utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, the 15th of January [sic], 2010. I would like to welcome our witness, General Petkovic. I would also like to greet the accused, as well as all the counsels and all the members of the OTP, as well as everyone helping us around this courtroom. Before handing down an oral decision, I would like to give the floor to the Registrar, who is going to give us two IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 4D and 2D have submitted their objections to the Prosecution's list of documents tendered via Witness 4D-AA. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01176 and 001177 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Oral decision dealing with a motion from the Petkovic Defence to add 16 documents on the 65 ter list, dated 15th of February, 2010. On the 10th of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence has filed a motion in which it asks the Chamber to add, on its 65 ter list, 16 documents which they intend to bring forward during the testimony of Milivoj Petkovic. During the hearing of the 11th of February, 2010, the Trial Chamber invited the Prosecution, as well as all other Defence teams, to send their response today. The Prosecution informed the Chamber, as well as the parties, that it was not going to be against the motion of the Petkovic Defence. The other teams from the Defence side have not issued any response. The Trial Chamber notes that the motion from the Petkovic Defence is extremely late, insofar as it happened one day before the testimony of Milivoj Petkovic. The Trial Chamber notes, however, that neither the Prosecution nor other Defence teams have brought forward any prejudice linked to this tardiness. The Trial Chamber has, therefore, reviewed this motion and feels that the 16 documents identified display prima facie indicia of reliability, probative value, and relevance. Consequently, the Trial Chamber decides to grant the motion and authorises those documents to be added. And I'm going to quote them: 3D02408, P03027, P05573, P06027, P06397, 4D01300, 4D01346, 4D01671, P01341, 4D02026, P02599, 3D00526, P00166, P02114, 4D02024, and 4D02025. These documents will be added on the 65 ter list of the Defence Petkovic. Judge Antonetti is adding a separate opinion to the current decision, and here is the separate opinion: The Trial Chamber decided to add on the 65 ter list 16 documents. I share fully this decision. However, I have a different opinion as to the third paragraph dealing with the tardiness of the motion, because as far as I'm concerned, this means that we don't really take into account the needs of the Defence, which requires constant interviews between an accused and their counsel, and it could well be that during those interviews the need could have arisen at the last minute to introduce a document for the needs of the case, because until now neither the counsel nor the accused would have felt the need or would have seen any interest in lodging this document, and during the interview this could have come about. As far as I'm concerned, Judges could not demand for all documents to be mentioned on the 65 ter list before a witness comes to testify because this would actually deny the rights of the Defence, which are enjoyed from the beginning of the trial to the end of the trial, and also during the phase where interviews are allowed between the accused and his or her counsel. This comment is also valid for the Prosecutor, who can also feel the need to introduce, at the last minute, a document for which a new interest has been identified during the proofing phase, as we call it. Therefore, in a criminal trial before an international jurisdiction, it could well be that the parties, namely, the Prosecution or the Defence, could feel the need, at the last minute, to bring forward a new witness, and, in fact, this document would not have been mentioned in the 65 ter list. And in this case, I do not feel that we should mention any criteria of tardiness which was mentioned in paragraph 3 of this above-mentioned decision. I feel that a Trial Chamber should display flexibility in case that it is faced with exceptional circumstances, and I believe that interviews between the Prosecutor and its witnesses or interviews between a counsel and his or her client, the accused, could lead to the need to introduce, at the last minute, an additional document. This is my separate opinion, bearing in mind that I fully agree with the fact that we've agreed with adding those 16 additional documents. Ms. Alaburic, the Registrar told me that you already used an hour and 19 minutes, so you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps before my learned friend addresses the Court, firstly, good afternoon. A very quick matter. Perhaps Your Honours could request the Registrar to contact the computer help desk. I did notify the Court that there was a problem before we sat, and that hasn't been rectified, so perhaps I could have some assistance. I would be very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please make sure that Mr. Khan can have access very quickly to everything on his computer. Very well. Mr. Khan, it will be dealt with. We have a very sufficient Registrar, so he's done everything that's required. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, Your Honours, and to the Prosecution, all the Defence teams. Good afternoon do you, General, and everybody else in the courtroom. I thank the Trial Chamber for its decision, and we can move on, General, with our discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The next section I'd like to deal with is the place of the Main Staff of the HVO in the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna, and let's start off with the documents. They're in the first binder, the second set of documents, and we're dealing with organisation and establishment. The first document is P289. It is a Decree on the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB, passed on the 3rd of July, 1992. My first question to you, General, is this: Did you take part in the preparation of this decree?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in the immediate drafting of this decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you present your views to anyone and say that the armed forces should be organised and what the role of the Main Staff of the HVO should be like?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the team working on this document did not ask for any opinion from the Main Staff about any issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In Article 2 of this decree, it says that: "The defence system of Herceg-Bosna shall be a unified form of organisation of the armed forces, administrative bodies, and legal entities, with a view to ensuring the timely and organised prevention of attack, or any other form of danger to the HZ-HB." Now, tell us, please, General, how do you understand this article? Does it mean that all the bodies of Herceg-Bosna play some role in defence, in the defence of Herceg-Bosna and Herceg-Bosna in general?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it means. That's quite -- that's a very normal and realistic article, and in other points the role of each body is set out for the defence of Herceg-Bosna, because all the bodies were established for one primary task, which was the defence of Herceg-Bosna or the defence of Croats living on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, was defence the reason for which Herceg-Bosna, itself, was established in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and according to what it says in the documents, Herceg-Bosna was established in order to defend the Croats and everybody else living in those parts, once an aggression against that area was expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in Article 10 of this decree, it says that: "The Defence Department shall perform staff and other professional work for the needs of the Presidency of the HZ-HB." And in Article 11, it goes on to say that for the performance of these duties within the Defence Department, the Main Staff shall be established. Tell us, please, General, to the best of your knowledge about this decree and its contents, except for the staff and other professional affairs mentioned here in this decree, were any other duties given to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, just this portion of the duties were placed under the responsibility of the Main Staff, that it be a staff organ of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Several months later, the decree was amended, and we come to the next document, P588, where we have these amendments of the 17th of October, 1992. Let me put right the number of the document. It is P588. So the amendments were adopted, and we have a new text of this decree. And we've already said that there was a misinterpretation of Article 10.2 of this decree, which relates to staff and other professional duties for the purposes of the Presidency of the HZ-HB. So, General, could you read out Article 10, item 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May we have Article 10, please, and for the English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says: "The Defence Department shall perform staff and other professional duties for the needs of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna within the frameworks of his remit in the area of Defence except for professional duties from the remit of other administrative bodies."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the mistranslation was that "staff duties" was translated as "command duties" in the first instance, and with that we have corrected that mistranslation. Now, in Article 9, we see that it refers to the tasks of the Croatian Defence Council, or later on, the Government of Herceg-Bosna. In your opinion, what was the most important task that the Government of Herceg-Bosna had?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Government of Herceg-Bosna, as indeed other bodies, within the frameworks of its duties and responsibilities, was the organiser and a body which, in a way, implemented the defence system. Its prime task, the one mentioned here, was to enact a defence plan for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which means that the government participated directly in the planning process. That's the first and most important duty. And let me say straight away that the defence plan, as a document, was never adopted, but there were partial documents which, during that war period, represented elements of that defence plan. Therefore, planning for the needs of defence is set here at the level of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, what is your position on the importance of the affairs and duties within the Defence Department? Of these many duties, which would you set aside as being the most important?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Article 10 sets out 24 very broad responsibilities and duties as tasks for the Defence Department, and I'd like to focus and set aside several of those. The first one is monitoring and co-ordinating activities aimed at achieving the agreed policy of the defence system; secondly, assessing the possibility of wartime and other dangers. And I'd like to add there that point 2 says "during wartime," and during a war it becomes an item which could read and would read as follows: "A reporting on the military security situation on the territory of the HZ-HB." The third point is making plans on the use of the armed forces. Point 4, setting up the system of leading and commanding of the armed forces in such a way whereby the system should be built up by passing the necessary acts and documents, and once these documents -- the first one was the Decree on the Armed Forces. And also the Defence Department adopted a number of documents and instructions which put things in their proper place, if I can put it that way, and thus influenced the control and command system. Furthermore --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. If I might interrupt you there. There's no need for us to read all the various items. I asked you what you thought was most important. So according to this decree, the remit of the Main Staff, did it remain the same, that is to say, that it should perform staff and other professional duties for the requirements of the Presidency of the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with respect to these amendments that were passed in October 1992, everything remained the same; that is to say, that the Main Staff should perform staff and professional duties for the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at the next document now, please, General, 4D12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when I look at this document, there are two articles, Article 9 and Article 10, that articles have to be interpreted according to their heading, and the heading is "The competencies of the HVO, administrative bodies of the HZ-HB." So a legal expert reading this may have the feeling that Article 9 deals, as far as the HVO is concerned, with everything that is listed from point 1 to point 8, and especially what is of the utmost interest is point 7; namely: "Draw up plans for preparation of the terrain for combat." So here we have the HVO, probably its military component, but at the same time I do not have any other details regarding this. So one could think that we have Mr. Mate Boban and perhaps others. And then you have Article 10, which is of a more administrative nature, and it has to do with the Defence Department or perhaps what we could call the Ministry of Defence, and here this is more technical or more administrative. We talk about the various measures and so on and so forth. And in Article 10, when we look at the Defence Department, we do not have the feeling that it has any operational role. As far as the operational area is concerned, it is point 7 of Article 9. So since you were on the ground, I was wondering whether Article 9 was giving Mate Boban the authority and perhaps giving the authority to others, and whether Article 10 is only dealing with the Defence Department, but it's in its administrative component and only that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Article 9 does not refer to Mate Boban as the supreme commander. Article 9 refers to the executive authority of the HVO. That's the first point. And point 7 that you mentioned, it says "should establish plans -- draw up plans for the preparation of the terrain for combat," not for defence. I think you read it out as being for defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There might be a problem of translation there. Could you read out paragraph 7 in your language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wondering whether you could read paragraph 7 of Article 9 in your language, not in Article 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am reading out Article 9.7. It says "Determines plans for preparing the territories."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the English translation, Mr. Karnavas, since you are an expert in the English language, is there not a problem in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's nothing about combat, so obviously whoever translated this into English wanted to put a burden on the government. And I don't know who is responsible for that, but the word "combat" is not in there, and I think it should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So there was a problem in the written translation. It's not going to be the only one. I'm sure there will be others. Given the problem with the written translation, my question is irrelevant. Ms. Alaburic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's look at the next document, 4D1287, which is the Law on Defence of the Republic of Croatia from 2002. Tell us, please, General, to the best of your knowledge, at the beginning of the 1990s in Herceg-Bosna, were the laws or decrees prepared in such a way that they were -- that laws adopted and used from the Republic of Croatia with certain amendments and modifications?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, the existing laws in the Republic of Croatia were used, and they were adapted to the situation in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at Article 11 of this document, General, to see how this was defined as far as the Main Staff was concerned in 2002, for the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia. And we'll see here that mention is made of 31 tasks for the Main Staff, and among those tasks, under item 6 we have: "Command of the armed forces in conformity with the orders given by the supreme commander and the minister of defence and his documents, and the promotion of the system for command and control of the armed forces," et cetera. My question to you, General, is this: If we compare these two decrees on the Law on the Defence of the Republic of Croatia, dated back to 2002, and the decree we saw a moment ago, which provision wants the Main Staff commander to be strong and have the main competencies?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a provision passed by the Republic of Croatia, compared to the decree passed by Herceg-Bosna, so these tasks were not defined in the Decree on the Armed Forces of Herceg-Bosna at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, General. P586 is the number. This a decision on the establishment of the Defence Department, and I'd like us to focus on item 9, which deals with the Main Staff and its organisation and establishment. We've read through this particular excerpt many times in this courtroom, and we've analysed it many times, but I'd like to hear your opinion. It says the chief is the head of the Main Staff and that the chief is responsible to the head of the Defence Department for certain duties and the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna for other duties, and the responsibility of the head of the Defence Department relates to all the administrative affairs and the question of budget and materiel resources and consumption, and the general establishment and life in peacetime and wartime organisation for the armed forces, and responsibility to the president of Herceg-Bosna, as the supreme commander. And it relates to all questions of supreme command, establishment, strategic and operational plans, and the use and deployment of the armed forces both in peacetime and in wartime. Tell us, please, General, according to your understanding of this, the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, was he really that responsible to the head of the Defence Department or, rather, the minister of Defence Department and for certain affairs to the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is precisely how it was, whether it's Article 9, item 9, but it doesn't speak about duties, but responsibilities, and that's how the responsibilities were set out. According to the tasks that came under the head of the Defence Department, the chief of the Main Staff was responsible to the head of the Defence Department. And the duties that came under the domain of the supreme commander, then he would be responsible to the supreme commander, everything that comes under his authority and responsibility. So from this it follows that the chief of the Main Staff has a dual responsibility. One is administrative affairs, vis-à-vis the Defence Department, and the other is vis-à-vis the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the following item, it is defined in which respects the Main Staff is superior to the command of the HVO, and it reads that it is superior in the -- within the scope of general and specific powers vested in him by the president of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, that this is about the general and the specific powers vested in him by the president, that is, the supreme commander, which means that the specific powers of the chief of staff are never outlined, but it's only defined in terms of vested in him by the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the next item deals with the responsibility of brigade commanders, so it says that brigade commanders shall be subordinate and responsible to the supreme commander or, alternatively, the head of the Department of Defence and the chief of Main Staff, within the scope of their responsibility and in accordance with the powers described above. Tell us, General, does this provision mean that direct communication between the commander-in-chief and brigade commanders is allowed or with the commanders of the zones of operations?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is mentioned here that the commanders of the brigades are subordinate to the president of the HZ-HB, as far as command responsibilities go, but the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that this says that the brigade commanders are subordinate and responsible to the president of the HZ-HB, as their supreme commander, and they are at the same time subordinate to the head for his responsibilities, his powers, and to the chief of Main Staff if these are the powers transferred to him by the commander-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honour. I would like to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said "the head," and in order to make it very clear, the head of what?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Department of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, we have here the last paragraph in the English version, which says that the brigade command are subordinated to the president of the Croatian Community, and they're also responsible to him, and the president of the Croatian Community is the supreme commander. Now, this, of course, has consequences regarding the command liability -- command responsibility and responsibility of a superior. Now, let's imagine that a brigade commander, Mr. X, directly calls Mate Boban and tells him, President, let me report to you on such and such situation. For example, unfortunately we shot at a house where there were civilians, and unfortunately these civilians were killed, and so forth and so on. And the president says, Well, it's nothing, no problem. You will be covered. So the commander of the brigade does not report this to the commander of his operational zone, nor to the chief of staff, because the information went from the commander of the brigade directly to Mate Boban, by passing the chain of command, and thus the chain of command is not aware of the problem, if we look at this text. Now, could you tell us whether things occurred in such a manner within the HVO or whether what is written here was only theoretical and was not applied practically on the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this order wasn't issued without a reason. It wasn't phrased this way by chance. The commander-in-chief was supposed to have direct communication with the brigades, and the reason is because, at the level of Herceg-Bosna in connection with these instructions, there were no strictly-defined duties of the Main Staff or the commander of the zone of operations. And the same applies to brigade commanders. This should all be contained in one document of the type -- as the same type as the document Croatia passed in 2000. So there were cases of brigade commanders addressing directly the commander-in-chief, or direct communication from the zone of operations commander to the commander-in-chief. So documents that were made at such times are not possible today, because everybody's role would have to be strictly defined from the chief of General Staff to the lower levels of command. I repeat that there was a document passed in the Republic of Croatia in 2000. There was a list of 30 duties. Under those, exhaustively defined the responsibilities and powers of that commander. In Herceg-Bosna, that was never done, or wasn't done at the time. Until 1994 or 1995, the Decree on the Armed Forces was not even amended. This was made in October 1992, and that's how it stayed until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand that you are confirming that even in the Republic of Croatia, brigade commanders could directly report to the president. And any reasonable trier of fact could infer from this, just like I do, that sometimes the chief of staff or the commander of the operational zone was not made aware of certain situations, he was bypassed given this system. Now, the following question: The text that we have here on brigade commanders, can it also be applied to the commander of professional units? To mention one, Mr. Naletilic. Does Mr. Naletilic belong to this whole system, i.e., he would report directly to the president, so he would be directly subordinated to the president of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and only be liable to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have so far been able to see that that was, indeed, the case. He was directly subordinate to the commander-in-chief, and he was responsible exclusively to him. Only with the approval of the commander-in-chief could he be used elsewhere, irrespective of the actual size of the unit at the time. But he was able to give his unit such a status, and he behaved that way throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe my fellow Judge has questions for you also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, please. It does not refer to Naletilic, but to the general rule. I must say I find it extremely confusing that there was a regulation according to which brigade commanders were submitted to the chief of the operation zone and, at the same time, also directly to the commander-in-chief. You have explained this by saying that the duties of the General Staff and its head were not strictly defined. I cannot understand why, in such a situation, one does not strictly define these duties so as to have clear structures. I would fear, if I put myself in the shoes of the persons concerned there, that such double line of command to brigade commanders risks creating the greatest insecurity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, well, that's not really the way it was allowed to happen. Let's assume that the commander-in-chief issued an order which obliged other people. So lower-level commanders, that is, brigade or operative zone commanders, are responsible to him who issued the order. That's normal. In another situation, if the commander-in-chief transfers powers to the chief of General Staff and says, You will prepare and conduct some combat activity in some area, then these are concrete tasks given to the chief, and the brigade commander will be responsible to the chief of staff. But I agree that this should have been put into writing much better, but it wasn't. You will have noticed that nobody mentions the operative zone here; only brigades. So the author of the document even left out the operative zone. We will see several such documents which were amended, but nobody ever added the operative zone, so it looks like we worked without the operative zone all the time. So this was somebody's omission which was never rectified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I must admit or I will admit that I am much more interested in what actually happened than in what was in the books. Could you tell the Chamber whether Mate Boban made use of the possibility to order brigades directly in many cases or in few cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't really say how many such situations there were, but there were situations in which they were issued an order from the commander-in-chief. Sometimes the commander-in-chief summoned them to him for a briefing about the situation in the brigade, and sometimes the Main Staff, on behalf of the commander-in-chief, would issue orders to the brigades or the operative zones. So there were situations of both types.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't find the second eventuality you mentioned problematic. If the supreme commander does this via the General Staff, that, to me, seems normal. If he does bypass the General Staff, would he at least serve the General Staff with a copy of his order or in some other way inform it properly of what he does with a unit that belongs to the Main Staff, actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all units are subordinate to the commander-in-chief. They're all his units. And then there are also units of the Main Staff and others down the chain of command. It is normal for the commander-in-chief to do what he deems appropriate. That's his right. But the commander-in-chief need not monitor the situation. He can issue an order, but he assigns the duty to the Main Staff to monitor a situation, because the commander-in-chief is an individual and cannot monitor the overall situation, whereas the Main Staff and the zone of operations are a group of people that can monitor the implementation of the supreme commander's orders. That's why it is said that the Main Staff is a staff organ of the supreme commander. That is to say that the Main Staff does all the work, because the supreme commander has nobody else to work for him except for the personnel of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I may add this: Each unit, from the brigade to the -- or the operative zone up to the supreme commander has its staff, and superior to the staff there is the commander. It's like this in the brigade and in the operative zone, and at the highest level, too, there is also a staff which is much bigger than lower-level staffs. And at the peak of the pyramid, there is always the commander. So much by way of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Not just not to hide, I confess or I state that I have served on the staffs of a division of what, in Switzerland, is called an army corps, three-star general, and in the General Staff of the army, so this corresponds to my experience also, whereas the other organisation does not. It is special, this possibility of a supreme commander giving directly orders to more than one step below. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you have answered in an extremely detailed way to a great number of questions, and I must ask a follow-up question, and I believe it's important. We see the system as you describe it, but this -- we must put this system in contrast with the indictment. So as an assumption, I would like to know whether it would have been possible that as of May 9 and the following days in 1993, Mate Boban would have given direct instructions to Naletilic. All words here are important. So did he give Naletilic a direct instruction, instructing him to collect the entire Muslim population of Mostar, to take them to the Velez Stadium and then to the Heliodrom, and could it be possible that Naletilic got the order and implemented the order without, and I insist on this "without," without the chief of staff -- the current chief of staff and the commander of the operational zone of Mostar being made aware of this? What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is difficult for me to answer a question like that, because in the morning, at 5.00 a.m., I wasn't in Mostar, myself, for me to be able to know who was given what assignment. I arrived eight or eight and a half hours after the initial combat operations had started. Now, as regards the relationship between Naletilic and Mate Boban, what I can tell you is this: From mid-November 1992 onwards, they had the following relationships: Mate Boban accepted the Convicts Battalion, he accepted Mladen Naletilic as his adviser through whom all relations with the Convicts Battalion and any possible beneficiaries of its services were solved by Mr. Naletilic in consultation with Mr. Mate Boban. And we'll come to why I mention mid-November 1992 as a date, because as of that date the Convicts Battalion was outside the Main Staff and outside any influence -- any Main Staff influence, that the Main Staff did not have any influence on the Convicts Battalion as of that time. And except for in July, the order that mentions them, there's not a single other order from the Main Staff which makes mention of the Convicts Battalion. And you were able to see the Ludvig Pavlovic and Bruno Busic and all the other ones were mentioned, and that is not without reason. And I hope that through our further discussions, we'll come to that subject, not to have to deal with it now. We'll deal with it in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, I put this question to you because when earlier you answered my fellow Judge - the page is no longer on the screen, but I will quote your answer from memory - you said that Mate Boban would give an order to a brigade commander, but that he could or he must - I don't remember whether you said he could or he must - make sure that the chief of staff actually carries out the order, as far as he's concerned. When I heard you saying this, I immediately thought about May 9th, with Naletilic collecting the Muslim population. And I wonder whether General Petkovic, if he wasn't there at 5.00 a.m. and arrived eight hours later, I really wondered whether General Petkovic had been made aware of what was going on, because this is what you said. And we now come to the core of the subject. I would like to know whether you were made aware of the fact that Naletilic was conducting an operation aimed at "isolating" -- I'm using this word in quotes, so to isolate a number of people -- a number of Muslims from Mostar, to isolate them at the Heliodrom. Were you made aware of this? And if so, could you tell us when, exactly at what time, to the minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one sentence before that. When I mentioned the brigade, I was not thinking of the Convicts Battalion, which didn't have the status of a brigade. It was 50 or 60 men. It was an independent unit, and it was given the name "battalion," but it wasn't actually a battalion. It was more a company. So when I spoke about a brigade, I certainly excluded that unit. I wasn't referring to that unit. And, secondly, when you're asking about Mostar and about my response, what I can tell you is that I did not receive an answer from the commander of the operative zone when we met in Mostar, telling me that somebody had done those acts towards the civilians, as you've just presented it here. The information that I received, when I asked whether there were any killed in Mostar and what happened to the civilians, the answer I was given was that the civilian population had been evacuated from the most threatened parts of town which were closest to the separation line, and you all know what that was - that was the Bulevar and the other part - and that such civilians were taken over by the civilian structures. Mention was made of three men who, at Heliodrom, took them in and took care of them and accommodated them. So as far as I was concerned, at that point in time it did not represent ethnic cleansing or any arrests or anything like that, anything that would be in violation of any conventions. As far as I was concerned, it was a piece of information received that, from the confrontation line in town, part of the population was pulled out and provisionally put up, but not under the administration of any segment of the army, but under the command of those who were in charge of social care for persons like that. And these were three individuals who took care of those people throughout who were put up at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This was a very important question, and you answered me in a very detailed way. However, you did not tell me at what time exactly you were told about this. When did you hear about it? Can I have a time? If you remember, of course. I fully understand that this was 15 years ago, so it could be difficult to remember such a detail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I arrived quite certainly in Mostar sometime after 1.00, by 1.30 at the latest. And by the time I contacted my operative zone commander and by the time I told him to come and see me, and when we started our talks, it could not have been later than 2.00. So during the half hour that I was there, I had to speak to the people whom I encountered down there, who knew what was going on, and then I told the operative zone commander to come in and give me -- and report to me and give me the information he had; that is to say, what I was interested in at that moment. So we can put it at sometime around 2.00 p.m., 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I got the answer to my question, but I believe my colleague also has a couple of questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. It's actually not a question of my own. We have a lot of text here, but I do not think that you have really answered the question Judge Antonetti put to you at the beginning of this series. It was a theoretical question. Do you consider it possible or absolutely impossible that Mr. Boban gave an order to Mr. Naletilic to the effect that he should take certain Muslims away from Mostar? I try to put it neutrally. And it's actually a yes-or-no question. You think it's absolutely excluded, even theoretically; or you think that perhaps theoretically it's not absolutely excluded, although perhaps quite unlikely? But the likelihood is not what I'm asking, just the abstract possibility or impossibility.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we said that Boban sent Tuta to Mostar, he couldn't have envisaged what was going to happen, and there's no reason for him to start out from thinking that some people had to be sent somewhere. Reason tells you whether you're going to do something or not. Now, when there was firing at residential buildings and when there was firing coming from balconies, people left their homes and went to take shelter and refuge in the entrances. And at that point in time these people had to be moved from those areas to some safer place or places. I do not believe that somebody in the morning could have thought along the lines of the fact that the operation could have escalated to such an extent and that what happened would have actually happened. I don't think they could have foreseen this in advance. As far as I know, the first evacuation of civilians, as far as I now remember, began at around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we just ask the general to repeat the first sentence of his answer, if you remember it, General, because as it is recorded in the transcript, it doesn't reflect what you said. So could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The question was about the theoretical abstract possibility of Boban really ordering Tuta to collect up the Muslims in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that he issued the order -- well, to issue the order to go to Mostar and round up the Muslims of Mostar. Nobody thought about any rounding up of Muslims in Mostar. So even had he given him a command on a theoretical level, it would not have been that kind of order, if that is an answer to the question. Can you read out that first sentence? Which first sentence do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, the essence is that you put it in the conditional, even if Boban had sent Tuta to Mostar, it did not mean that he would issued an order to him to round up the Muslims, because in the early morning nobody knew how -- what the developments would be, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's it, that's it. If he sent him, nobody could have known what was going to happen. Something happened three or four hours after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to our analysis of the various provisions. We're going to skip over two documents because time is flying, and let's look at P7236 now, please, 7236. It is a decision on the establishment of the Ministry of Defence, and the date is December 1993. And let's see whether the relationships were the same. It is regulated by Articles 11 to 13, where repeated mention is made of the fact that the chief of the Main Staff shall be responsible to the minister of defence for certain affairs and to the president of Herceg-Bosna for other affairs, and also in para 2 of Article 13, that the chief of the Main Staff shall be superior to the commands of the armed forces within the competence of the chief and specific authorisations from the president of the Republic. Now, to the best of your recollections, General, in the provisions governing the position and role of the chief of staff and the armed forces, did anything change while you were in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing essential changed in those provisions, and in this particular document this is divided into several articles. Otherwise, the text is almost completely the same or similar to the ones we looked at previously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, which is 4D1605, and this is a command or order from December 1993 again from the then minister of defence, Perica Jukic, in which the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, it says, shall report to him, and what those reports should be like is set out in the document; that regular meetings should be held with his assistants and commanders of the military districts. Now, tell us, please, General, are you familiar with this document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It's a document signed by the new minister or, rather, Minister Perica Jukic, perhaps a month after he took up his position as minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who was the chief of the Main Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the chief of the Main Staff at the time was General Ante Roso.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know, General, whether Ante Roso actually did report to the minister of defence in this way?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that, because the defence minister gave specific tasks both to the Main Staff, with respect to work and analyses and meetings in the Main Staff, and with respect to its duties -- or his duty to travel around the military district. So the minister made full use of his powers, regardless of the fact that nothing had changed under the law. The minister did have the right to order something like that because the minister had to receive reports about the situation in the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document now, please. It is P4699, and it is a report on work for the first half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Forgive me, Ms. Alaburic. I have a question of translation. In the first line, under the heading "Command," it is said: "Each Monday of the month, the head of the General Staff shall report ..." Is that the correct translation or should it say "each first Monday of the month," because the words "of the month" make no sense if it should be each Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under item 1, I read: "The head of -- the chief of General Staff of the Croatian Defence Council shall, on each Monday of the month, report to me on operational/tactical situation with proposals for improvement in work procedures and in accordance with the following points:" And then the points follow. It does not say "every first Monday." Actually, reports were sent to the minister four times a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, during our analysis of these documents please bear in mind that those were times of war and that these documents were not written by persons who were linguistically very apt, so this causes problems to us lawyers. But these were mostly not written by lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P4699, we said this is a report on activities. In the introductory remarks or notes, in paragraph 4 we see that the military and security situation on the territory of the HZ-HB was a priority in the work of the HVO HZ-HB and was given special treatment. As far as you know, General, did the individual bodies of Herceg-Bosna do their utmost for that part of Herceg-Bosna to defend itself against the aggression?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most certainly that was the priority and everybody's work. The military and security situation on the territory of the HZ-HB was the factor that determined everything else there. And this is June 1993, which was the most difficult period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know this document, General?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because I also submitted part of this document, contributed part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This part of the document, when you say that, you mean the report on the activity of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an integral part of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, does this document faithfully reflect the remit of the individual bodies of Herceg-Bosna in dealing with issues of various types?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was duty-bound to draft reports about the things from his remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It follows from this report that the Department of the Interior was in charge of public security, law and order. As far as you know, was it really the case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the foremost task of the Department of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, P3642. This is your condensed report for six months, which, on the 22nd of July, 1993, you submitted to the head of the Department of Defence. You have seen this document in this courtroom frequently, and the Judges had numerous questions about it. I just wish you to explain to us item 4-6. When you speak about problems, you say, I quote: "The expectation that the HVO army will resolve everything by itself militarily and on the front-line, that is to be expected and that is, indeed, the task of the army. We still do not have such an army with a modern organisation that is technically well equipped, with a dedicated command system. In order to create such an army, the authorities must do far more at all levels, and this must be their primary task. Practice teaches us that the army is becoming privatised. Every municipality, every town and village, have their 'own' army. It isn't possible to move a municipal army from the area of the municipality, and by that very fact the deployment of stronger forces adequate to the task is not possible." As far as you know, General, in mid-1993, can the military of the HVO be considered a well-organised and well-trained army in which the chain of command, the chain of reporting functioned well, and which would be comparable to the military of a more highly-developed country, say one from Western Europe?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly not. This was written 15 months after the establishment of the HVO. Fifteen months are not enough to establish the kind of army you have described; organised, trained, ready to carry out its duties. But work was being invested for the army to be better every day, but of course it wasn't possible to achieve that in 15 months. I'm not saying, however, that from the beginning to that time, no progress was made, but that progress was not sufficient for us to be able to call that army well trained, organised, and well equipped, especially the latter part. In spite of all efforts to take that military out of the hands of some local forces, we were unable to do much. I'm not saying that all municipalities were a problem, but in the more important municipalities, which were financially stronger, we were unable to achieve anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, if I remember well, the Prlic Defence tried, during their defence case, to show what difficulties the Herceg-Bosna authorities were facing to get insight into the situation on the ground at all, because the municipalities were there, they had been there from former times, and they were very powerful, and the presidents of the municipalities were members of the legislative body that had the power to appoint and to dismiss the members of the HVO, that is, the Cabinet, so these were all problems the civilian authorities were facing. Tell us, did the situation affect the army too?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it most certainly did. The civilian authorities at the level of Herceg-Bosna were not able to assert themselves in all issues to the local authorities, because the civilian authorities didn't have money or anything and everything took place at the level of one municipality, and the municipality would say, We do that ourselves and we have to decide about all that ourselves. And their position was, We are defending our municipality, so why don't you let us do so? And in such a situation, the executive structures were powerless. Financially -- or, rather, it may sound funny if I say that the municipalities were financially stronger than you were, but they were. And they were able to do much more for their soldiers, such as paying them, providing health-care, et cetera; whereas at the level of Herceg-Bosna you didn't have that kind of money, and even if you did have some money, you couldn't exert such an influence. And then you also said that they were members of the Presidency. That was another problem, because some people would say, You're not talking to me as the president of the municipality, but be aware that I also have a second hat, that of a member of the HZ-HB, so that the Cabinet actually couldn't go about its work. And some people, individuals, made use of that; not all of them, but some did in their respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I will now skip what is very clear from the decree, but let's take a look at the following document, P293. It's a rule book, the Rules of Military Discipline. Tell us, in one sentence, did these rules enable military commanders to punish their soldiers fast and efficiently, and also NCOs and officers, if they were breaking the law?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are some provisions to that effect, but these rules were not implemented as they should have been. The most important element, namely, military tribunals, were not established in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, now we'll be brief; short questions, short answers. What was the term used for slight breaches of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were called "disciplinary infringements."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what were more serious breaches of military discipline called?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Disciplinary offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who had the right to decide about holding somebody responsible for these disciplinary offences?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme commander had that authority for all officers. Well, actually, it was the Court for Military Discipline. That Court was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What kind of breaches of military discipline were within the remit of military commanders?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military commanders decided about slight breaches of military discipline, and the disciplinary measures they imposed were very mild and actually inappropriate for wartime. They may have been appropriate in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could military commanders place an officer or NCO of theirs in military detention for breaches of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, military detention is for soldiers and reserve soldiers, these two categories only. They were susceptible to being placed in military detention. But officers and NCOs were not. They could be reprimanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, Article 67 of this document stipulates who can pass the decision to bring the offender before the Military Disciplinary Court, and it says, under 1: "The commander of the armed forces for higher-ranking officers." And, secondly: "The commander of the operative zone for non-commissioned officers and officers up to a certain rank." General, it follows from this that the chief of Main Staff was not in the position to issue a decision to bring an offender before a military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that is what this provision says.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the following document now, 4D1346. It's a rule book on military discipline that was in force for the Armed Forces of the Republic of Croatia. It is from 1992. Let us look at Article 69 to see how it was regulated in Croatia. In Croatia, these powers were vested in: One, the chief of the Main Staff for higher-ranking officers; and, secondly, the commander of the operative zone for non-commissioned officers and officers. These two documents are almost identical, except in this part, because in Herceg-Bosna the chief of Main Staff does -- explicitly does not have the right to bring offenders to a military court, and that right is vested in the commander of the armed forces. Do you think, General, that this legal provision was meant to strengthen or weaken the position of the chief of Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia, the position of chief of General Staff was certainly strengthened, but in Herceg-Bosna it was weakened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I have a number of short questions about remit. As far as you know, General, was the chief of Main Staff involved in taking decisions about the organisation and the powers of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the chief -- or did the chief of Main Staff have the power to decide about using military or civilian police for combat purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, did the chief of Main Staff have the power to decide about issues within the remit of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could the chief of Main Staff decide about issues from the remit of the SIS?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could the chief of Main Staff decide about issues within the remit of the IPD?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't have that power.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could the chief of Main Staff decide about -- decide about criminal proceedings, prosecution, and other issues having to do with military jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, could the chief of Main Staff decide about establishing prisons, or detention facilities, or any other facilities for detaining persons?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't have that power.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the chief of Main Staff have the power to decide about managing and controlling prisons, detention facilities, and other detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't have those powers, nor did he exercise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could the chief of Main Staff take measures and decide about issues that have to do with public law and order?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, public law and order is not part of the authority of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have done -- I'm done with this part. Perhaps we could have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we've just been speaking about what was not under the remit of the chief of the Main Staff. Now we're going to deal with what was under the authority of the Main Staff or were linked to the authority and remit of the Main Staff, and we're going to start off with the crime base situation. And let's look at the first document. 4D1355 is the number to start off with. This is your interview which appeared in the "Vecernji List" in August 1994, when you were leaving Herceg-Bosna. Before I ask my questions based on this document, just a question. In your response here to the second question, you say that in coming to Herceg-Bosna, or, rather, Bosnia-Herzegovina, you thought that you would stay for about a month while the problem at Kupres and Livno was resolved, but that, nonetheless, you stayed for more than two years. Now, tell us, was that your intention in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, that's what I thought. I thought that it would last for a brief period, because in the neighbouring municipality in the Republic of Croatia, UNPROFOR forces had already deployed, and it was to be expected that with the proclamation of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the UNPROFOR forces would be deployed there, too, in similar fashion. That's what we expected, but it never came about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in this interview, General, in answer to a question about the results of the war with the Muslims, that they were worse than the results of the war with the Serbs, you say that you did not prepare to go to war against the Muslims. Now, today, General, when you're here at this Tribunal and in this courtroom, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether the HVO really did not prepare for war with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't. The HVO did not prepare at all for a war against the Muslims. The HVO wanted the Muslims and Croats to unite as far as possible and to stop the Serb attack or to extend the free territory, depending on the political will of the leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 1D2340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, in this interview which you gave at the time, were you answering questions put to you by a reporter? Obviously, through his questions, he seemed to be well informed of the situation. In this interview, you explained that at one point in time there was also General Praljak, and you talk about the areas covered. General Praljak told us on several occasions that there had been an allocation of territory between you and him, so could you tell us what exactly was your territorial competence? What was your area of competence, in terms of territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we didn't divide up the territory in any way so that we could say that one person was responsible for this and the other for that. The situation, itself, in Central Bosnia, and the fact that instead of General Praljak, I went to the negotiations, imposed the need for me at that time, while spending time in Central Bosnia, to use the opportunity to learn as much as possible about the events in Central Bosnia, to try and contact the people as much as possible, because I was the only person who, with the help of UNPROFOR, was able to reach Central Bosnia and the Kiseljak area alone. Everything else was -- well, the UNPROFOR could -- well, except in one case they refused to help me to go to Busovaca, Travnik, Vitez, and so on, and in that context General Praljak passed on the authority to me, following talks, and I went to Central Bosnia quite often. And therefore it was normal that apart from the tripartite or bilateral talks, that I take care of the situation with the HVO in that area, to deal with that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you've answered my question. In this interview, you seem to express surprise, as well as General Praljak was also surprised, when Ante Roso replaced General Praljak. Do you confirm that you were surprised by this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to be quite frank, I did not expect General Roso to arrive at the place he arrived at, and that news and the appointment of Ante Roso took me by surprise. I don't know whether General Praljak knew or did not know. If he did know, he couldn't have known one or two days before -- before one or two days before. I don't assume that there was talk of this 10 days before and that, therefore -- because if that had been the case, I would have known about it. But we didn't expect Ante Roso to come, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last item. Well, I could ask a great number of questions, of course, but time is of the essence. So this reporter seems to be well aware of things, and he's asking you some questions about the Old Bridge and the destruction of the Old Bridge. You answer his questions, and I'm interested in his last question on this topic and your answer: "Let Mr. Military Prosecutor continue his job." I checked to see the date of this interview. It was on August 2nd, 1994, early in August 1994. The Old Bridge had been destroyed for several months already. So when you answered this, did you know -- obviously, you knew that there was a military investigation underway and the military prosecutor was in charge of investigating this and trying to find the truth? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, we did know -- or, rather, it was known that the military prosecutor had raised an indictment against three or four soldiers, and that he conducted an investigation, and the investigation went along the lines -- well, the military prosecutor kept the investigation to himself. How far he got, I don't know. But apart from those three or four, I don't think he got any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within this investigation led by the military prosecutor, were you summoned to be heard as a witness or did anyone think it was useless to put any questions to you? I'm talking about the investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, nobody summoned me as a witness. All I know is that the commander of the operative zone's presence was required, and he did state his views. And everything else, the investigation took place in the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the only thing you know is the commander of the operational zone was heard, but you were not heard. Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether he was heard, his testimony was heard. All I know is that the operative zone commander said that his presence was required, and the commander of the operative zone compiled a list of three or four topics and sent them out to three or four addressees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless I'm very much mistaken, we went into that with Vinko Maric, one of our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, the next document, 1D2340, is the transcript of a TV programme called "Close-Up." I'm interested in page 19 of the Croatian and page 23 of the English text of the transcript of that programme. K. Zubak says, with respect to the conflict with the Muslims: "We were absolutely not ready and prepared, and the situation came about without us being prepared to react." Now, tell us, General, we see what Kresimir Zubak says, that the HVO was not preparing to war against the Muslims. Now, in your opinion and to the best of your knowledge, was that the general position in Herceg-Bosna, or do you know of anybody who did want to have a conflict and was preparing for a conflict with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was the general position. At no point did we prepare for war against the Muslims. Quite the contrary, we tried in all manner possible to draw as close to them as possible and unite at all levels, to unite our forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us, as you understand the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in Herceg-Bosna, when did the conflict start, when did an all-out conflict start?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have my views on the matter. After the unsuccessful de-blockade of Sarajevo at the end of December 1992, according to my information, the Muslim political leadership had a rift, there were difference of opinion; as existed in the military leadership, too. And both the political and the military component was afraid of the unsuccessful efforts on the part of the Muslims in the conflict with the Serbs. And since the de-blockade of Sarajevo was to serve as a major victory over the Serbs, which would turn the course of the war around and which, in a way, would dictate negotiations in January in Geneva, that never happened. And so ways and means were sought for the BH Army to score successes to boost the morale of the army in any way possible. However, unfortunately, as far as we were concerned, these conflicts started between the Muslims and Croats. And confirmation of this is my talks with Mr. Izetbegovic, when, on the 14th of December, 1992, he called me to come to Jablanica and talk to him there, and also to talk to his command, which was preparing to lift the siege of Sarajevo from the outer limits, because the de-blockade of Sarajevo took place externally and internally. And on that occasion, Mr. Izetbegovic told me that he expected to score a great victory which would reverberate in Europe and the world and which would affect the outcome of future negotiations. And when I said, Why Sarajevo, Mr. Izetbegovic, it's a big bite in the middle of winter, he said, Well, if I don't liberate the political centre, everything else is less important. And so they expected a lot to come of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, General, what your answer to my question is. When did the conflict take on a broader scale between the Croats and the Muslims and on a more permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it began from the Geneva negotiations in January, and they burgeoned and took on greater intensity and expanded from Vakuf to Busovaca and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the January conflicts, were they stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The January conflicts were stopped, first of all, in Vakuf, and then, to everybody's general surprise, they broke out in Busovaca. And I can say, quite frankly, that we were defeated and that the HVO, as a compact part, was separated into two parts: Kiseljak, Kresevo, and Fojnica, they were separated from Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik, and Novi Travnik with a corridor which was seven to ten kilometres wide.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise, General, but we don't have time to go into an extensive explanation of the situation. But tell us, if the conflicts were stopped in January 1993, does that mean that the conflicts weren't any -- weren't lasting, didn't last for a long time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, because the efforts that Halilovic and I invested, they were stopped, and we thought that the problem of the conflict between the Croats and Muslims had been resolved. However, we then had March and April of 1993 and the events that took place at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say March and April happened, March and April of 1993, what event are you thinking of specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm thinking about the 23rd of March, 1993, and the attack by the BH Army against the HVO in Konjic at a time when the negotiations in Geneva were going on, and two days before Mr. Izetbegovic finally signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, repeat the date once again. It wasn't recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with the Konjic events in due course, but just one explanation here. When you spoke to us about the fact that you had information to the effect that the Muslim leadership, after the unsuccessful blockade of Sarajevo, was going to prepare another action which they hoped would be successful to boost morale in the BH Army, are you actually referring to the information you obtained after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, part of the information was information I received on that 14th of December, 1992, when Mr. Izetbegovic called me to go to Jablanica to see him, and in the interim General -- well, they called him -- they referred to him as "Talijan," the Italian, but I think his name was Bajram Hajrulahovic. He came up to me and said, Petkovic, what we're going to ask of you, please assist me there, because if we don't succeed, it won't be a good situation for either you or us. And from that, I deduced that success -- the success of the Sarajevo operation could determine the future course of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, after this operation had been completed, what happened, quite simply, was that there was a conflict among the Muslim units, themselves, which had taken part in the de-blocking of Sarajevo, and at the same time I met Mr. Hajrulahovic -- or, rather, we had talks again in July 1994. When I visited Sarajevo, I was reminded of my talks with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you then, on the occasion of that visit in 1994, learn that the plan was to achieve that victory in fighting the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted a victory over the HVO. Otherwise, they were afraid that their system of control and command and their army to start falling apart. Their conclusion was, The Serbs are very strong, and we can't stand up to them, but the Croats are weaker and isolated, and we can beat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you learned about that at that meeting in 1994 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The man was sincere because he had already fallen from grace, the grace of the members of the BiH Army and the people of the 1st Corps, because they were singled out as the culprits for the failure of the lifting of the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did the conflict at Konjic on the 23rd of March end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic. I would like to ask a question relating to the meeting on 14 December in Jablanica. Hearing this and considering the situation, of course, from a great distance, the question occurred to me whether a joint attack to liberate Sarajevo, HVO and Muslims, whether that was ever taken into consideration, and, if so, why it was obviously decided against.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the 14th of December it was considered to attack Sarajevo in order to lift the siege, and that is why Mr. Izetbegovic invited me to that meeting. And I joined the staff of the ABiH, which was preparing that operation. Mr. Izetbegovic and the gentlemen from the staff raised some demands, to call them that, toward the HVO, and we did what they wanted, to some extent. They wanted our brigade to join them in Sarajevo, which was done, and our forces from Konjic to get involved, which was also done. They also wanted ammunition from me, and that was also done within two days, and subsequently in phases. And they wanted, I think, 500 rifles for Pasalic to enable him to arm an equal number of men willing to fight, and they had been -- they had left the municipalities of Eastern Herzegovina. And those were their demands toward us. They were saying that they had 11 brigades in Sarajevo, that was the strength of the first brigade. And they had a number of brigades around Sarajevo on the -- facing the besieging forces. And everything was agreed. On the same evening, after the meeting, I left for Grude. I informed Mr. Stojic and Mr. Boban on the following day, and Mr. Stojic insisted that we should equip Pasalic to the best of -- as best we could. And I think we gave him some 300 rifles, as many as we had. We gave him equipment, clothes, and ammunitions, the quantity of ammunition that we had in stock at the time. What's more, we ordered our brigades to send some of their ammunition toward Jablanica to Konjic from where the operation was supposed to be launched. So Mr. Izetbegovic was surprised by our promises, what we would do for him. And then he promised he would invite me to the launch of the operation, but he failed to do that. Obviously, they wanted to surprise me, too. So I was at Sarajevo Airport when the operation started. There was a tripartite meeting scheduled there, a meeting of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. They had already started the lifting of the siege of Sarajevo, and that's exactly the time when they started -- were starting the operation. And for two days, the fighting went on with full intensity, and that was the most serious attempt to lift the siege of Sarajevo until that time. There was one in October, but that was more of a political nature, but this one was real, and they really did start lifting the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
