utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to use my right to pass on this information to my Defence team. This is military information about which we could ask General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just an observation on the transcript. On page 45, lines 23 following, I read the following: "They were saying they had 11 brigades in Sarajevo. That was the strength of their first brigade." This confuses me somewhat. Could you clarify? Perhaps lost in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was a mistranslation. These 11 brigades in Sarajevo were part of the 1st Corps, which had its headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, there was this meeting with Izetbegovic on December 14th. Could you tell me which year it was held? Was it 1993 or 1994? Maybe 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, in 1992. I listened very carefully to what you were saying in order to understand how the events unfolded, and there are several levels that we don't have. But you were at the first level, you were at a very high level. The first level would be the politicians of the time, President Clinton; the British prime minister; Mr. Mitterand, the late Mr. Mitterand. That's the first level. The second level is the level of the negotiators in Geneva, Mr. Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen, but nobody believed that it was important enough to ask them to come here. And then there's the third level, and there's four of you in that third level; yourself, Halilovic, General Morillon, and Mr. Thebault. That is the third level that could be used to try and understand what actually occurred. In the first level, I did not include those who passed away, Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic. So you were one of the main actors in this third level. And while you were answering a question put to you by Ms. Alaburic, you said that on December 14th, 1992, you met with Mr. Izetbegovic to try and devise a plan for Sarajevo in order to help lift the blockade of the Serbs over Sarajevo and, therefore, to disengage the ABiH. I was listening to what you were saying, and if it's true, it's fine. If it's not, of course, Mr. Scott, during his cross-examination, will, I'm sure, demonstrate this. But right now, you're under oath and you're supposedly telling the truth. So when you met with Izetbegovic, it is because Izetbegovic believed that you were one of the military components of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's HVO, and there we're back to the old debate regarding the components of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And earlier you explained at length that there were 300 rifles that were handed over, Pasalic, and so on and so forth. I'll spare you the details. And then you say that at that moment, Izetbegovic understood that he would not be able to gain any results, vis-à-vis the Serbs, because of the power of the Serbs. I was trying to read in between lines there. And so for him to have better standing in front of the international community, his only alternative -- his only option was to attack the HVO, and it's this way around and not the other way around. So by saying this, of course, you're going against the case of the Prosecution. You say that they attacked you, and you say that it was because the HVO was in an inferior situation as compared to the BH Army; it was easier for the BH Army to win fighting with you than fighting the Serbs. And I'm finally coming to my question. You were in contact with all these negotiators in Geneva, so when you found this out from Mr. Izetbegovic's mouth, did you convey that message? Did you say that there was a double deal here; that, on the one hand, seemingly one party wanted peace, but was waging war against you? Did you say that? And if you did convey that, who did you convey it to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me put it this way: Mr. Izetbegovic really invited me on the 13th, but I wasn't able to come on that day. A message was left for me to meet him on the 14th in Jablanica, and I really did come to that meeting. I considered it my duty to respond to his invitation, because he was the president of the Presidency, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, irrespective of my view of the HVO. Sarajevo was some 150 kilometres away from Jablanica, and still I went off to meet him there. And Mr. Izetbegovic and his staff told me what they wanted to achieve and how. They wanted all possible assistance and materiel at that moment. They wanted the HVO to assist them by giving ammunition of different calibres. And our neighbour from Mostar, Mr. Pasalic, asked for a quantity of rifles to be provided to him to enable as big a number of his soldiers from Mostar as possible to also take part in lifting the blockade, and that's all we could do. And in the first 20 minutes of his meeting, in a separate office while his personnel was preparing the meeting, he was able to explain to me what he wanted. He said, Mr. Petkovic, we opted for such a massive and demanding operation of lifting the siege of Sarajevo because we want to come to Geneva with a big victory on our hands, and then we will dictate our conditions for peace negotiations to the Serbs. And then I asked him, Well, Mr. Izetbegovic, can't you see what the weather's like? Igman and Bjelasnica, where the main axis of attack was to be, there was over a metre of snow there. But it was their position that they would do it that way. A Prosecution witness from Jablanica confirmed that I was present at the meeting, and he said, with a smile, that they never actually showed me the plans -- the maps with the plans, but the only question that they had for me was how I could assist them, in terms of materiel. And I promised that I would give them everything that we had, and that he was quite surprised by that. And I think that he actually expressed his gratitude to me and to the HVO for having done that, in spite of the failure of the operation. And let me prove that by saying that I went with him to Geneva for the talks. He actually flew me there in his own aircraft. After this failure, Your Honours, that resulted in a route, his units being routed, and there were substantial casualties in the clash on Mount Igman, and all the reports conveyed the idea that they were in a difficult situation. And instead of having a victory under their belt for the talks, they went there with this massive defeat they had suffered in the effort to lift the siege of Sarajevo. And after that, at some points in time the BH Army actually turned to the HVO to attack it, and after that operation there is no -- there are no major operations against the VRS, not even in Eastern Bosnia, where the situation in Zepa and Srebrenica and in other areas was really difficult. The 2nd Corps was immobile, doing nothing. And from that time onwards, all the activities, in the intervals that we have seen, were all targeting the HVO. Unfortunately, from March onwards, they were quite successful in their operations against us, and I could even say that we were down to two small enclaves in Central Bosnia. All the rest fell into the hands of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army. And the position of their people is, We cannot fight the Serbs, because they are very strong, but we can fight the Croats. So they were actually looking for space in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Central Bosnia, and that's how this conflict came into being. We discussed with Mr. Boban, Mr. Akmadzic, who was in the Cabinet at the time, in the government, the situation that developed. And I think that in late December, even Mr. Prlic sent a letter saying, Why is the BH Army pursuing a different line than the politicians in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time? He issued a warning of sorts in this letter. So this is, in brief, what I have to say to you about the lifting the siege of Sarajevo. They failed to do that. And after that, a number of clashes with the HVO followed. I can also tell you that on the 20th and the 21st of December, Mr. Stoltenberg was in Sarajevo - 1992, that's the year I'm talking about - and that I and the other two commands, Mladic and Halilovic, were invited, through the good offices of General Morillon, to attend a meeting, a preparatory meeting for the Geneva talks, because they were scheduled to go on within a couple of days. Mr. Halilovic did not attend, and I, myself, had been blackmailed by General Mladic in the following way: Mladic was to arrive in the Lukavica Barracks first, and once he was taken by UNPROFOR safely there, then they could take Petkovic to Kiseljak, because there were detonations around the airport at the time, the BH Army was attacking the Serbian forces at the time to no avail, but that was on the 2nd [realtime transcript read in error "22nd"] of December, 1992, when I and the other two commanders were invited to come to Sarajevo for the talks, and we expected Mr. Stoltenberg to arrive for this preparatory meeting for Geneva which was supposed to start in early January 1993. Halilovic did not attend the meeting, so that for all intents and purposes, this attempt to achieve an agreement among the three commanders, which was supposed to speed up the talks on military issues in Geneva, fell through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you've added some details. Maybe there is a mistake in the transcript. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make one clarification. On page 47, line 22, you indicated, Mr. President, that no one thought it was important to invite certain persons such as Lord Owen. Let me make it very, very clear for you, Mr. President. We did make every effort possible to bring Lord Owen here. He refused to come and testify for any side. So I want to make sure the record is rather clear. We do make efforts, and sometimes we're unsuccessful. We sought not to have him subpoenaed, because we don't think it's advisable to try to subpoena somebody who doesn't wish to come and testify here, someone at least of that calibre. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. But as far as I'm concerned, I would have had no problem to subpoena him, or anybody else, actually. General Petkovic, you made some clarification, and we discovered that a meeting was planned with Mr. Stoltenberg and General Mladic, as well as Mr. Halilovic, who was supposed to attend, but Mr. Halilovic did not show up. Does that mean that it would explain that the ABiH, as early as January, would launch an attack in Central Bosnia in some areas that were held by the HVO? And if so, could you tell me which areas those were, because we were not in the tu quoque here, we are looking at a diplomatic explanation of an international conference, and we were trying to see who's playing what here. So according to you, the ABiH has launched an attack against which areas; in January, that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have seen that on the 6th of January, 1993, the first clashes in Gornji Vakuf erupted. That was the last day of the conference, the first part of the conference in January 1993. Likewise, on the 11th -- the night between the 11th and the 12th of January, 1993, again the conflicts in Gornji Vakuf were renewed, and the 12th is the first day -- or the last day of the second part of the talks in Geneva. And let me say that on the 26th -- or, rather, from the 23rd and the 26th of January, we went to Geneva again, and from the 25th until the 28th, there was an attack on an area between Busovaca and Kiseljak, where the HVO was pushed back from a rather large area, and this resulted in the enclaves of the Croatian population in Central Bosnia. Those clashes were stopped thanks to the efforts of myself and Mr. Halilovic, but BH Army forces did not pull back to restore the state as it was before. And it is interesting that all those clashes erupted to coincide with the talks, so on the 23rd of January, a couple of days before Mr. Izetbegovic was supposed to affix his signature to the Vance-Owen Plan in New York. He signed it on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Alaburic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two corrections. At page 49, line 6, the word "Sarajevo" should be erased, and there should be "Usora," it should read "Usora." And at page 52 -- "Usora," well, it's okay. Page 52, line 9, the date is supposed to be the 22nd of December, not the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what you said, but it's not been recorded correctly in the transcript. Now it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I'd just like to avoid any misunderstandings in an effort to understand what you know about the plans of the BH Army to put a stop to the conflicts with the Serbs or, rather, not to launch any attacks to liberate its territory from the Serbs, but rather to target the HVO. Correct me if I'm wrong, you learnt that, in 1994, that was how it was formulated in the talks at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we learnt that already in January 1993, through our intelligence efforts, by monitoring their conversations, and in 1994 I visited Mr. Hajrulahovic in his apartment in Sarajevo, and that's when I learnt that. In that conversation, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think that we were at the question of how the conflict that erupted on the 23rd of March, 1993, in the Konjic area was actually stopped.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd, there was an attack by the BH Army on the HVO units in the Konjic municipality. I called Mr. Pasalic in the evening of that day to ask him what was going on in the Konjic municipality and why those things were happening, and we wrote a joint order and sent it to Konjic in order to put a stop to the conflict there. However, I decided -- and I agreed with Mr. Stojic that the best thing to do would be to go to the Konjic area, because we were concerned that the clash in Konjic might affect the final round of talks in New York. And on the 25th, we actually arrived in the municipality of Konjic. Pasalic was there, too. So were two SDA members from Mostar. And there, on the spot, we talked to their people in Konjic. Safet Cibo appeared there for the first time, and he was the one who actually initiated the clashes. And we managed to actually put a stop to the clashes on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did clashes again erupt in the same area one month later in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, less than a month. On the 13th of April -- well, I wouldn't say that there was a clash that erupted. I would say that the conflicts actually escalated, because between the 25th of March and the 13th of April, despite the presence of our emissaries there, they did not manage to put a stop to the BH Army attacks everywhere. So between the 25th of March and the 13th, there was still fighting for some villages where the Croats were forced to retreat because they were in the minority, and on the 13th the signal came for them to liberate the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us, you, as the chief of the Main Staff, did you issue an order to any operational zone or any HVO unit to assist the HVO units in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did, because the thought that was foremost in my mind was who would be in a position to assist, because the municipality of Konjic and the HVO in that municipality was not adjacent to any HVO units in the other municipalities, so between the municipality of Konjic and the municipality of Prozor, there is a wide area controlled by the BH Army. To the north, likewise, from Konjic to Kresevo and Kiseljak, there is an area -- intermediate area where the HVO units were not adjacent, that were not controlled by them, so my first thought was, Who could do it? At first, I thought that it would be best to engage the forces in Fojnica and in Kresevo and in Kiseljak from the north, to launch any kind of "show of force" attack or any kind of "show of force" military activity. That was on the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you issued an order to the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia to assist Konjic. Could you please answer, General. So did you issue an order to the Central Bosnia Operational Zone?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, I did issue an order to the Central Bosnia Operational Zone to use an element of its forces from Fojnica, Kresevo, and Kiseljak to engage in any kind of operation they could in the Konjic municipality. First, they were supposed to reinforce the sector there, and then they were supposed to launch an operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you to be as brief as you can in your responses. If there's any need for us to go into any details, I'll be asking you follow-up questions. Tell us, please, General, did you issue an order to help Konjic and the operative zone of Zeljko Siljeg and Miljenko Lasic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't issue any specific orders to them at the time because Miljenko Lasic, himself, took certain steps, because Konjic was in the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, and Zeljko Siljeg, only on the 16th, that is to say, on the fourth day -- or, rather, four days after the beginning of the conflict, arrived in Prozor and set about organising a forward command post to assist Konjic, as the closest.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, did you have information about combat operations in the Konjic and Jablanica area in mid-April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, we did have information, and it was daily information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose was of armed engagement in HVO units in the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to push back and repel the aggression or an attack by the BH Army against two brigades, Herceg Stjepan -- two Herceg Stjepan brigades in the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell us what the purpose of combat -- HVO combat was in the Jablanica area.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Konjic and Jablanica represent a whole. You can't separate the two, in military terms. The same goal, to lift the siege or, rather, to help the HVO forces in Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, a question directly related to the indictment now. The Prosecution's case is that the HVO started combat operations in order to take control of Jablanica. Can you tell us, to the best of your knowledge, whether the HVO ever planned to take control of Jablanica, and the combat activities, do they have anything at all to do with some idea of taking control of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, the HVO never planned to take control of Jablanica, nor did the HVO have the forces and strength to do so. Everything that the HVO did was in terms of assistance to HVO forces in Konjic municipality which found themselves in a situation that they couldn't deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the explanation you gave earlier on, when you say "Konjic municipality," that you mean Jablanica municipality as well?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Konjic and Jablanica municipality, you can't separate the two, you can't say, This is Jablanica municipality and that's Konjic municipality. You can't separate the two, in military terms, because an HVO brigade on the Konjic-Jablanica territory, the BH Army, with three brigades of the 4th Army [as interpreted], covered the Jablanica-Konjic area, and you can't separate the two in any way, by any measures or anything else. It is one area, and they are each dependent on the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to talk about the Jablanica-Konjic area so that we don't have any problems a month to come, whether you're talking about Konjic or Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I say refers to Konjic and Jablanica as a whole, as one entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, look at the next document, which is to be found in the next set of documents. It is 4D2025. So we're skipping five documents -- or, rather, three documents, and we now come to a map which was prepared on the basis of document 2D246, which is an order of the 44th Mountain Brigade of the BH Army, dated the 14th of April, 1993, about combat engagement for certain units. Now, tell us, please, General, who drew this map?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did. I drew the map pursuant to an order from the 44th Jablanica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, does this map show the situation in mid-April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map shows the situation as of the 14th -- between the 14th and 15th of April and further on, so the 14th, in the evening, and the 15th, in the morning. This map refers, first of all, to the night between the 14th and 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, since we're interested in this map principally because of the indictment as referring to Sovici and Doljani, could you try and explain to us where in the Sovici and Doljani area, or just in one of those places, were the units of the HVO? And can we give the general something to indicate on the map, a pen or pointer?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's zoom in to the central part of the map, where the markings are, the coloured section in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that sufficient or can we zoom in some more?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, it's sufficient, but I'm not sure that others will be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Time is expiring quickly, so please tell us, General, where the HVO units were.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO units were located in the blue area. I don't know if you can see it [marks]. It says "HVO," and this is around Doljani and a part Sovici, in Doljani and part of Sovici. It was the Mijat Tomic HVO Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us the following: The HVO forces to the left of that, and we can see that they're coming in here to an area close to Sovici and Doljani, what's that, which of those?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These forces over here [marks], and this is what that was about: On the evening of the 15th, and I'm talking about the 15th of April, 1993, the 44th Brigade of the BH Army in Jablanica placed the HVO in Doljani under a complete siege, and the HVO forces were pulled out in the area of Risovac, with the aim of preventing possible further expansion by the BH Army towards Risovac or, rather, Blidinje Lake or Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, can you explain to us what happened on the 17th of April, 1993, in the early-morning hours?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say that on the 16th, in the evening, the Command of the Mijat Tomic Brigade talked to the Command of the 4th Battalion of the BH Army. They discussed lifting the siege from the Sovici gates. They refused to do that. And then in the morning, this left-hand arrow over here [marks] indicates an attack launched at the HVO positions at Risovac. And at that moment, the HVO responded by attacking the Sovici gates. And I'll place the number 1 there, which is where the Sovici gates are [marks]. And the fighting went on there, as far as I know, for about three hours, along these axes to the left and right of the Sovici gates. The BH Army, I don't know for what reason, withdrew from the Sovici gates to Sovici proper, and it found itself in a situation whereby it didn't know what to do next. It did not organise a defence in Sovici, itself, but at the Mijat Tomic Battalion's call to them to surrender, the commander of the 4th Battalion decided to surrender his forces at Sovici, so that there was no direct fighting between the HVO and the BH Army for the town of Sovici, itself, because the BH Army, after its withdrawal from the Sovici gates, did not succeed in organising a defence for the town of Sovici. Some of the people fled to the nearby municipality of Prozor, and the rest were not ready to organise a defence at that time, and so they surrendered in the classical way. The BH Army surrendered without any fighting for control of Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, in a word, what happened to Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO in Doljani refuted an attempt by the BH Army from the Jablanica axis to attack, and the forces of the brigade from Jablanica withdrew, they left the area. And part of the population fled with them, or, rather, left the area with them, so that the forces from Jablanica did nothing. And they were supposed to be reinforcement to the BH Army in Sovici, so that now Sovici found itself in a situation in which they had the HVO to their rear in Doljani, and the commander, Orlovic, decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if we were to summarise, in the simplest terms, General, could we do it this way: There was no fighting in Doljani because the BH Army withdrew from Doljani, and in Sovici, itself, there was no fighting, either, because the BH Army surrendered, and the fighting took place around the Sovici gates, where the HVO units broke through the lines held by the BH Army up until then. Would those be the three main points in that summary, in the summary of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, with that, on the 17th of April, 1993, did the conflicts and clashes in this Risovac area and the Sovici gates area cease?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the fighting ceased on the 17th, as we like to say, in the area of Sovici and Doljani with very small forces at three small points up in the hills above Doljani and Sovici from where this group of people tried to fire on Sovici and Doljani, but the fighting ended with the surrender of the 4th Battalion sometime in the afternoon, in late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, some HVO units, did they try to uncover these BH Army groups that failed to surrender which were in the surrounding hills somewhere? Is that what they tried to do?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who made this decision to enter into this undertaking, because it was a high altitude, 900 metres above sea level, and it was a tremendous task and not an opportune one, so that HVO soldiers were killed, in my view, needlessly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, in those operations was the commander of the Convicts Battalion killed, Cikota?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cikota was killed on the 20th, I think, around Elevation 902, on the 20th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, on the basis of the information the Main Staff had, up until that point in time in Sovici and Doljani, those places, themselves, did any member of the HVO commit anything that could be considered as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, you have been discussing the question of Doljani and Sovici and the fighting around those villages, and you may recall that a few days ago -- and also the death of Convicts Battalion head Cikota was also mentioned, and we saw a document over there in which it was also pointed out that that event happened during a kind of cleansing or cleaning, "cistka," of Sovici, so I would like to ask Mr. Petkovic if he would tell us what kind of actions took place, I mean armed actions, in Sovici, and why the reference to cleaning, cleansing, "cistka ," was mentioned in that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel Your Honour -- I apologise, not Trechsel, Prandler. In Sovici, there was no fighting to take control of the place of Sovici, itself. Now, whether there was sporadic fire by a group of individuals, I really don't know. But Sovici, as such, were handed over without a battle. They surrendered without a battle. Secondly, when you say "cistka," c-i-s-t-k-a, two or three points which -- at positions in the mountains above Doljani and Sovici, I think they were Feature 902, I think that was Elevation 902, there were two or three members of the army there, BH Army, and as far as I remember now a place called Pisvir, also two or three or five BH Army members. And from those elevations, they opened fire on Sovici and Doljani. Mostly Doljani, rather than Sovici. Now, I don't know who made this mad decision to send a group of several HVO members to, as we call it, cleanse Pisvir and Feature 902, because it belonged to the Doljani area, so there was no cleansing in Doljani. And in the terminology of the JNA, in JNA terms, "ciscenje," "cleansing," means finding stragglers and groups of enemy soldiers, and nothing more than that. That's what JNA terminology ascribes to the term "ciscenje," "cleansing." So they were killed on those elevations above Sovici and Doljani, and looking at the map, I think the position was closer to Doljani than Sovici. But Cikota wasn't killed in the -- in Doljani, proper, but at a distance of 700 or 900 metres, at an elevation of 700 to 900 metres above Doljani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petkovic. Actually, I used the Russian equivalent "cistka" for "ciscenje," but, of course, you understood this as well. So thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may remind you, in this context, that in our expert report, the report of Mr. Milan Gorjanc, one chapter is about this very topic, and we have pointed out that the translation of this term as "cleansing" is wrong, because it should be properly called "mop-up operations," because "cleansing" is associative of ethnic cleansing, but which has nothing to do with what really happened. Mop-up operations are normal in any army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, until the moment Cikota was killed, and according to the information that arrived at the Main Staff, did any HVO soldier do anything irregular, undesired, or illegal in the area of Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Everything that I read that referred to the 19th, 20th, and 21st was to the effect that anything of that kind took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us about after Cikota's death.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Cikota's death, a group of members of the Convicts Battalion and a group of civilians that didn't belong anywhere returned to Doljani after the funeral, that is, to Sovici and Doljani, and started burning some Muslim houses as vengeance. But I must say that the Convicts Battalion, on the 20th, officially withdrew from the front-line, and nobody counted on it anymore in case there should be additional fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, did you request information about that from the HVO Brigade Herceg Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But be brief.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on behalf of Mr. Boban. There is a document which we have already seen here. He wanted accurate information as to what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you receive such information from the Herceg Stjepan Brigade as to what had happened at Sovici and Doljani?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we received such information from the Herceg Stjepan Brigade, which was in charge of the Konjic municipality, and from the Mijat Tomic unit, which was also active in the areas of Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you forward that information to the commander-in-chief, Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he demanded that information. And that information, as well as the information I had prepared for Central Bosnia, I gave to him when I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to the supreme commander about the measures to take against these individuals from the Convicts Battalion who had taken part in the burning of the houses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed measures because we were preparing for a meeting in Zagreb and that was a topic that we had to discuss, so we spoke about measures. And the report that we received pointed out two names. One of them was Naletilic, and the other -- what's his name again, his assistant in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ivan Andabak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, did Mate Boban say that he would establish the possible responsibility of some individuals and take care of the situation, or did you have any related task?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, before the witness answers, I've been letting it go all day, but I'm going to object to leading at this point. The witness should be allowed to speak for himself on his own memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're absolutely right, Mr. Scott. I was a bit shocked myself. You know, instead of saying this, you should have said, What did Boban do? Here, you were prompting the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was not my intention to ask the witness what Mr. Boban did. I wanted to ask him about his conversation with Boban, because if they spoke about the establishment of responsibility, what was agreed, whether Mate Boban would do anything about it or possibly General Petkovic. My question contained several options, so, by definition, is not leading. A third option in General Petkovic's answer is also possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This was clearly a leading question, Ms. Alaburic, and I'm afraid you have to accept this. No one's perfect. Try to ask what Boban said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honours, although it is very difficult for me to accept that my question was leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, General, tell us, did you speak with Mate Boban about establishing the individual responsibility of anybody from the Convicts Battalion who took part in burning houses?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The names from the report were presented to Mate Boban, the names, and it was clear that two individuals were responsible for that behaviour, and the third one, although indirectly, the battalion commander at Doljani, Mr. Stipe Bolo, anyway, confessed that he was also co-responsible, but he couldn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would the possible proceedings against Mladen Naletilic and Ivan Andabak be within your authority?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We went to Zagreb with this information and this knowledge, to the meeting that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, do you have any knowledge about Mate Boban initiating proceedings to establish the responsibility of members of the Convicts Battalion for the burning of houses in the Sovici and Doljani area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing concrete. I only know that Mr. Boban, at the meeting in Zagreb, committed himself to do something about it and probe into the matter in the days to come, the following days.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, General. Let me now ask you about some events from April up until the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the question of Sovici and Doljani, as you know, is at the core of things, among others. Now, according to what you're saying, and I heard you very carefully - you know, as soon as you talk, I am listening - this is how I understood the military situation: In Doljani, the HVO carried out an action, and you showed that on the map. The BH Army soldiers did not fight and just withdraw, and they leave for Sovici, they withdraw to Sovici. The HVO continues fighting, and you say that the soldiers surrendered, and you said that they surrendered without fighting. While you were saying this, I noted a contradiction with the death of Cikota. Cikota died. It's probably because there was at least an exchange of fire. So why did you say that they surrendered without fighting, when Cikota was actually killed? Can you shed some light on this, because there's something that I probably misunderstood or didn't understand at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you may have misunderstood me, or possibly you haven't understood all I said. There was fighting at the Sovici gate and at positions to the left and to the right of the Sovici gate, which is some two or three kilometres away from the village of Sovici. That's where the defence line of the ABiH was. You weren't there. If the Sovici gate is taken, it's like going from the fifth floor to the basement, Sovici and Doljani are in the basement. And the fighting at Sovici gate lasted for three hours, at least. Once the Sovici gate had fallen, the 4th Battalion of the ABiH was lost. They were only able to raise some 80 people or so who surrendered. Everybody else fled in all directions. And when the HVO descended to Sovici and Doljani, the ABiH didn't put up any resistance. They had accepted the order to surrender. So there was fighting on the route towards Sovici, and when that defence fell, that was the fall of Sovici too. And Cikota, on the 20th - I don't know on whose orders - went to take out two or three enemy firing positions in the hills around that village, and that's where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your answer is very straightforward. I understood you very well. I have another question. The military operation on Doljani and Sovici, well, could you tell us under whose command this operation was, whose it was? Who was in charge of this military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doljani and Sovici were under the command of the commander of the Zone of Operations of South-East Herzegovina, Mr. Lasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And you learn that some houses were torched, civilian houses, so you know that there's a problem, especially if those houses were not torched because of combat, but for another reason. Wasn't it up to Mr. Lasic to live up to this responsibility? Wasn't he first in line there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I know, Mr. Lasic, too, was at Mr. Cikota's funeral on that day, and after the funeral he went to his command post. He didn't know what happened after his arrival. It wasn't the whole Convicts Battalion who went up there, only a group of people and a group of civilians. After the funeral, Lasic returned to his zone of operations, so that he learned about the event in the early-evening hours, after having received reports from Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, this is your version of the facts, and this is under oath, you say that what happened after Mr. Cikota's funeral was done by part of the Convicts Battalion, not the entire Convicts Battalion, but some of them, with some civilians who at the time were not identified. Then you talk to Mr. Boban about this, and he tells you, Well, we'll carry out an investigation, but he's not giving you any instructions -- specific instructions on this, so it's quite blurry. Now, you were in Geneva a couple of times. You were in contact with Halilovic, Izetbegovic, all these senior representatives, and maybe -- it's just an assumption, you know, I'm not in your head, of course not, but maybe you saw what the consequences could be if the foreign media found out about that. You know, you know what happened at Ahmici, and maybe you thought that there could be consequences to this. So did you envisage all the diplomatic consequences of such acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, clearly that was being taken into consideration, absolutely, how this would reverberate, and of course it didn't suit the HVO at all, the more so since the fighting had been over. Because of the death of one man, no such thing should have been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My final question. I would like to know whether it wouldn't have been possible to arrest a few members of the Convicts Battalion, to arrest also a number of civilians, hand them over to either the military prosecutor or the civilian prosecutor to make sure that there would be prosecution in such cases. Wasn't it a possibility just to arrest a few people in order to reassure the victims, the international community, and to prove your good faith, to prove that you, in true good faith, wanted to fight against crime? Why wasn't anybody arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the day when we received the report, the 23rd, we spoke about all that. The two persons to whom this referred most were Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Andabak. With this information, we left for Zagreb on the 24th, to that famous meeting that took place on the 24th and the 25th, and we spoke to Mr. Izetbegovic about everything that had taken place there; not only in Sovici and Doljani, but also Central Bosnia. There was a discussion about that for the entire evening, and the conclusion was that both sides would start clearing up these things. And it was signed, and by signing, the sides committed themselves to that. Once we returned from Zagreb, we held a meeting on the 29th or 28th - I'm not sure now - and at a meeting of the leading political figures of Herceg-Bosna a briefing was held about what had been agreed in Zagreb, and one item said that a commission would be appointed which, independently from anybody, would investigate the matter and take some measures, and that's what happened. I wasn't at the meeting of the 29th because I was in Zenica with Halilovic, or in Central Bosnia. But once I returned, I saw the conclusions from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is interesting, what you're saying right now. You've said that in Zagreb, all of this was touched upon, and everyone agreed, including Mr. Izetbegovic, for a commission to look into those "crimes," quote/unquote, and all parties would shed light on what happened, and you did not personally follow that up because you were in Zenica on the 29th. Now, let's talk about the commission. What were its conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commission, which was put into place on the 24th of September [as interpreted], was supposed to take all investigative steps in Herzegovina and Central Bosnia on the part of the Croatian Defence Council, that is, without waiting for the work of a joint commission, or there was talk in Zagreb for a mixed commission with the international community should undertake to resolve the problem. However, the proposal fell through. Nobody counted on it. So it remained for everybody to resolve the problem and deal with it at their own level. And the investigations for certain areas, on the part of the HVO, were put in place. They were unleashed, and they went on until about June, the 10th of June or 12th of June, when, in Central Bosnia, Travnik happened, with everything that that entailed. And then everything slowed down and came to a standstill. But we have documents about how this developed for Central Bosnia, but we don't have anything on how it developed in Northern Herzegovina or, rather, Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction to the transcript. On this page, line 5, the date was the 24th of September recorded there, but the witness was talking about the 29th of April, the 29th of April, and the meeting that took place, 1993, to avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't look at the clock. We need to have our second break. We'll have a 20-minute break, and we will resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. First of all, an administrative announcement. The Registry announced that the hearing that was planned on the 16th of March, it would be a morning hearing, will be cancelled because there are more trials than there are courtrooms, and so we have to actually have less days per week per trial. So Tuesday, the 16th of March, there won't be any hearing for this trial. So I wanted to announce that to you. Secondly, I understood that General Petkovic's Defence wanted to know when I would ask my questions. I am planning to do exactly what I did when General Praljak took the stand; namely, that I will ask my questions at the end of the examination-in-chief. I have planned two days for that. The first day, as already mentioned, will be devoted to questions based on documents from the Prosecution, and I will mainly base my questions on the pre-trial brief from the Prosecution. And as for General Petkovic, I will go through the indictment especially dealing with the JCE, and then I will show two videos. The first one is dealing with the attack against the Vranica building, in order to get the observations from -- or the comments from the general, and the second one will be a video of the destruction of the bridge in Mostar, because I will have very technical questions to ask to General Petkovic based upon this video. Then I will go through about 100 documents coming from the Prosecution. Most of those documents start with the letter P. Those documents will be showed to you in chronological order. I will start with a document dated 1992, and then I will go closer to today. For the second day, it will be exactly the same. There will be documents based on the submissions from the General Petkovic Defence. There's about 80 or 90 documents, 90, that is, and I will also present those documents in chronological order. So we will scan through 1992, 1993, and 1994, and this should take about two days. So this is what I can say at this juncture. Also, as early as tomorrow, I will send to all the parties, namely the Prosecutor as well as the General Petkovic Defence, I will send, as I was saying, the list of all documents, so you will have the various numbers for the first day and for the second day. That way, you will know exactly which documents I will base my questions on. Those documents have already been looked into and have already been the subject of discussions, but I may look at them from a different point of view. So this is what I wanted to say, and I believe this will be useful for all. I also should like to point out, since we are in this administrative part, on Thursday we will finish at 6.00 p.m. Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, Judge Antonetti asked you a question, recorded on page 71, about whether you took into consideration the diplomatic circumstances linked to the crimes in Ahmici and Sovici, and you readily answered and said that you did take into account the diplomatic activities. Now, since I have to recognise that I didn't understand either the question or the answer, does that mean that there was the desire to cover up something for somebody's interests or whether what was wanted was to conduct an investigation into the crime? So could you please explain your answer. What diplomatic interests, and in what sense were they taken into account, in care of, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, two or three days later we had a meeting with the top representatives of the community for the former Yugoslavia, and the whole problem was presented to them, that is to say, the events in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina. Lord Owen, as far as I can remember, had ten of his people at the meeting, attending the meeting, too, and both sides frankly presented certain matters and issues, so nobody kept anything back. So that's what I meant when I said "diplomatic." We didn't ask for ambassadors or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't a matter of wanting to cover up any crimes or keep something back?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And the meeting went on for quite a long time, and everybody was included. I'd just like to say that - and perhaps you can find this in the transcripts - Lord Owen said at one point, Take care that none of this should be counterproductive, thinking of the promises made by both sides that they would punish perpetrators and so on. So I remember him saying that. And perhaps you can find it somewhere in the transcripts of those meetings. So, no, nothing was kept hidden.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, when you mentioned the commission and the meeting of the 29th of April [realtime transcript read in error "January"], 1993 -- yes, the 29th of April, 1993, is the date. I'd like to correct the date. The 29th of April, 1993. Yes, that's right. What meeting was it that was held on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mate Boban, Your Honours, convened a meeting of all the relevant political factors in Herceg-Bosna, including the representatives of the Croats in the legal organs of authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the meeting discussed the Zagreb meeting, which had adopted -- or, rather, the conclusions of the Zagreb meeting had been adopted. And then with respect to the item on conducting an investigation, it was agreed that a commission would be established which, on the HVO side, would conduct all the investigations for the situations that happened until that time, whether there are five or six, in the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us again, General, where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th, I left with Mr. Thebault and Mr. Halilovic to Jablanica and Konjic and then to Zenica. On the 29th, I was in Zenica, and I was in Zenica on the 30th as well, of April, that is, of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now summarise this topic of Sovici and Doljani. During the combat, itself, General, in the Sovici and Doljani area, to the best of your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm going to object to this procedure. I think it's, again, a form of leading. There's really no reason for a summary. The Chamber's heard the evidence. It's not necessary for Ms. Alaburic to come back and put her spin on it, her summary. The Chamber has the witness's evidence. That's all that's necessary. I would object to this procedure. Formally, I object that it's a form of leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to ask questions, but I consider that I do have the right to use the time for our defence by devoting it to one topic, and if I need to clarify it, I can do for as long as I deem necessary. And I'm doing that because Judge Antonetti said that things were not quite clear to him and that he cannot link up what happened when, and the interrelationships, and so on. So instead of asking in redirect, I have to ask follow-up questions following on from the questions put by Their Honours, and I think it will be more efficacious for the Judges for us to clear it up straight away and not wait for the redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So my question to you, General, is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, that doesn't answer anything. The question of time and the question of what's more efficacious has nothing to do with the Rules of Procedure, the Rules of Evidence. If she thinks that clarification is necessary, she can ask non-leading questions, the general can give answers to non-leading questions, and we can proceed that way. That's the proper way to proceed, not by leading questions. And I continue to object.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't asked the question yet, so I would like to ask Mr. Scott to be patient enough to hear my question out first, and if it's leading, I'll be happy to apologise and revise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, during the combat operations of the 17th of April, 1993, in the area of Sovici and Doljani, were any houses set fire to, or, to the best of your knowledge, were there any unlawful acts committed by the HVO members?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, there were no acts which would be considered unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, General, when, in the area around Sovici and Doljani, were houses burnt, the houses of some Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, that happened on the 21st, in the late afternoon hours, the 21st of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Could we get some foundation for this as well? What's the basis for this information? We know that Mr. Petkovic wasn't in the area, apparently, according to his testimony, so what's the basis of the views that he's expressing now? Perhaps counsel can assist us by asking questions, laying a foundation for this knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm asking all these questions based on adjudicated facts adopted by this Trial Chamber at the proposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not my question -- that's not my objection, Your Honour. I don't really care what the basis of her questions are. I'm concerned about the basis for the witness's testimony. On what basis does this witness express a view? He wasn't there. We've talked about investigations. We don't know if there were any results of the investigation. He should tell us more. Did he receive a report, did he receive information, was there an investigation? Otherwise, this is sheer speculation, with no basis in the record for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, in order to avoid problems, please do like I do; namely, ask a general question so that eventually you reach your objective. You could perhaps ask him what happened on the 21st of April, Do you know of anything that happened? He could say, I do know, or, I don't know. If he says, Yes, I do know about something, then you could ask, What do you know? And therefore the Prosecution will not stand up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to acknowledge that I'm really surprised, because for an hour already we've been discussing the fact that General Petkovic, on the basis of a request from Mate Boban, sent a question to the Herceg Stjepan Brigade about events on the ground. The general told us that from the Herceg Stjepan Brigade, he received information about the events on the ground to the effect that after the funeral of Commander Cikota, houses belonging to some Muslims were burnt in Sovici and Doljani, and that it was some of the members of the Convicts Battalion and civilians took part in this. And the witness told us that it was on that basis that he prepared a piece of information for Mate Boban about that. The witness next told us about his talks with Mate Boban on the issue. The witness also said that this was discussed at a meeting in Zagreb on the 24th and 25th of April, and that the meeting was attended by the presiding office for the former Yugoslavia. The witness next told us that this was also discussed at a meeting in Citluk on the 29th of April, 1993, and that because of all these events, it was decided that a commission be established to investigate war crimes. So I'd just like to advise you to read the transcript from today's session, and it will be quite clear as to what the witness was talking about and what he said. And I wish to round off the topic exclusively, because Judge Antonetti said some things remained unclear to him, so it's my intention now quite simply to repeat that part of the testimony. Otherwise, I think that we have clarified all the points. With the previous witness, we put documents to him about all that, so I can't put all the documents to every single witness. I don't have time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So my question to you, General, is as follows: According to your information, the members of which HVO unit took part in the burning of houses belonging to some Muslims in Doljani and Sovici?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some members of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, the Convicts Battalion, was it in the command sense and in the operational sense, subordinated to the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't subordinated to the Main Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, on assumption that civilians took part in the burning of these houses, too, I would like to ask you the following: Did the Main Staff of the HVO -- was it in charge of prosecuting civilians if they engaged in unlawful acts?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not the Main Staff that was in charge of prosecuting civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's see how the combat operations ensued. Can you tell us whether anything important happened with the town of Kakanj in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1993, the BH Army placed the town of Kakanj exclusively under its control. It disarmed part of the HVO and expelled another part of it, including 12.000 -- approximately 12.000 Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether the BH Army took control of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the BH Army did take control of Travnik, and that was after the 8th of June -- between the 8th of June and the 12th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when did the BH Army take control of the area north of East Mostar or, rather, the Vrapcici-Bijelo Polje area and the other areas towards Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was taken control of on the 30th of June, 1993, by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I've listened to the question and the answer regarding Kakanj. You said that 12.000 Croats were expelled. This is the actual number that struck me. It seems to be quite a high number. The ABiH has launched a military action which will then be extended to Travnik. Given what is happening, at your level have you decided to inform the international community, because all this has consequences on what is happening in Geneva and on the various plans? As far as you are concerned, are you whistle-blowing, so to say, because this leads to flows of refugees, because 12.000 people, this is quite a huge amount of people on the road? What are you doing, faced with this situation? Are you just looking on, or are you acting on this by contacting Thebault, Morillon, Halilovic, and so on and so forth? What had you decided to do at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, first of all, in Travnik, on the 9th of June, I asked for a meeting with Sefer Halilovic anywhere, either in Sarajevo or in Kiseljak or in Zenica, and on the 9th of June, 1993, I arrived in Kiseljak because I had been informed that the meeting would take place in Kiseljak. Also coming to the meeting was Colonel Siber. I asked him, Why him? And he said, Well, don't you know what's happening in Sarajevo? And I said, No, I don't. Then I asked him, I said, Do you have the authority to sign a document with me? And Colonel Siber said, I don't know what my fate will be to the end of the day. Or, rather, on that day there was an exchange or rotation whereby Rasim Delic came to take over from Sefer Halilovic, so that neither of them arrived on that occasion. I prepared to return, but General Morillon asked me to stay on, and said that he would go to Sarajevo and convince Mr. Izetbegovic and Delic to come to the meeting. And that's what happened. The next day, Rasim Delic arrived, and that was his first meeting since he had become the new man to head the Main Staff of the BH Army. And on the 10th, Mr. Thebault was there, representing the observer mission, and there was also Brigadier -- I can't remember his name, but he was from UNPROFOR. And General Morillon remained in Sarajevo. And then Delic and I signed an agreement, and, among other things, we agreed that the joint command, six of them, should travel to Travnik and to try and stop further fighting in Travnik. However, the fighting could not be stopped at that point because two HVO brigades had been completely routed, and the inhabitants of Travnik -- and please don't hold me to the number, you can check it out, but in my view there were about 15.000 to 20.000 people who found themselves in the area between Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez. They stretched across that area. But a portion of them across Mount Vlasic fled. They were expelled to the territory of Republika Srpska. I think it was about 1500 of them, civilians; and about 650 soldiers. So that was the situation in April [as interpreted]. And linked to that, Mr. Boban sent a letter to Lord Owen and informed him that he would refuse to come to the Geneva negotiations because things like that were happening. And you know that there were negotiations in Geneva, and you saw the document which Mr. Izetbegovic, on the 15th of June, sent to me from Geneva. So that Boban had correspondence with Lord Owen, he informed him of the situation that was taking place in the Travnik area. Not long afterwards, suddenly Kakanj occurred. Just three or four days after Travnik, you had Kakanj. Once again, about 12.000 Croats had to leave the area, and that was what the situation was. In my view, it no longer gave any certain hope of stopping these events through negotiations, the events between -- that were happening between the BH Army and the HVO. And let me just add this: Mr. Boban put it to Lord Owen that Mr. Izetbegovic had waited for the Serb side to refuse to sign the Vance-Owen Plan, and as soon as the Serbs refused, one or two days later the BH Army launched its operation against Travnik. So there was no more Vance-Owen Plan, and now, in the interim, before a new plan got underway, they took advantage to take control of new territory and make it appear as them saying, There's nobody else and we're there. And the BH Army attacked the HVO in Travnik. We were the weaker side there, because the BH Army had a large number of brigades, and we weren't able to defend ourselves in a built-up area. We were taken by complete surprise. We simply didn't expect anything like that to happen. And to be quite frank, we didn't have the strength to resist in a town -- to defend ourselves in a town with a mixed population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, for interrupting. But I think before it leaves the screen, or it's about to, there was a reference on page 84, line 7, to April, and I assume Mr. Petkovic is referring to June, but, in any event, not April. Perhaps if that could be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. You are right, it's about June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott, for your co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let's see what happened later in various territories. Did anything happen in July with one of the two Croatian enclaves in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The enclave in the area of Klis, that's the Neretvica Valley. We've heard about Klis, on the 10th of July, disappeared for good, and along with it 1.000 to 2.000 Croats and about 350 soldiers of the HVO. In the Konjic municipality, what remained is a small enclave, and three smallest villages of Konjic municipality, Turije, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje, that's that famous pocket outside Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petkovic, I'm listening to your version of the facts and how, according to you, they unfolded; Travnik, Kakanj, Klis. And one can imagine what is happening, militarily-wise. And while listening to the description you're giving us, I'm wondering the following: In General Praljak's maps, we saw that the HVO and the BH Army had a joint front-line facing the Serbs. Maybe we can take a look at that map again, but I'm sure you know exactly which map I'm talking about. Now, given the actions undertaken by the BH Army, why is it that the HVO, who was on the front-line, didn't decide to withdraw to reinforce Croat positions that were under jeopardy? Why didn't you just withdraw from the front-line, leaving the Serbs facing the BH Army, in order to position yourself so you could reinforce your lines and so you could withstand the offensive carried out by the BH Army? Why didn't you decide on that line of conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me tell you the way -- how the BH Army took Travnik. They first attacked those HVO units that were -- had positions against the VRS, and thus they took positions against the VRS and the HVO was pushed back. In such a situation, the HVO has nobody but the BiH Army surrounding them. So at Travnik, the HVO lost contact with the VRS, and that was the intention of the BH Army. The first attack was along the front-line, take the positions against the VRS, and push back the HVO to make impossible any contact with the VRS, and that's what happened. Some soldiers and civilians were able to reach Vlasic, but then the area was sealed off. There, the HVO no longer had contact with the VRS. Now there was only the BiH Army that had contact with the VRS, and we were pushed back to parts of the Novi Travnik municipality and the municipalities of Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're giving me an answer for Travnik, but what about the other areas where the BH Army and the HVO were side by side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at that moment the BiH Army no longer sees a common enemy. It is focused only on the Croats. At Kakanj, we had lost contact with the VRS, so it was an easy job for the army -- the BiH Army, because there was 700 HVO soldiers. We had neglected that brigade because it was very deep in that territory, and it didn't require special equipment. And they took Kakanj easily in three days. In early July, they took Fojnica, and until the 10th of July, the municipality of Konjic. And we were left in that small pocket of Konjic with some 300 soldiers, and we stayed there until the end of the war. Not even Silajdzic was able to buy us with 5.000 [as interpreted] marks and persuade us to leave the area. That was how the BH Army went about it. They didn't want us to have contact with anybody. So that's how we fared in Central Bosnia. But we weren't strong enough to manoeuvre from one direction to another, because as soon as we would start any movement, we would be faced with BiH Army units that would prevent us from doing so. So we can't move from one area to another, and we cannot go from Herzegovina to Central Bosnia. We don't have enough forces to take 40 kilometres of area all the way to Novi Travnik, nor could we go as far as Konjic. The 40.000 soldiers of the HVO cannot take up the BiH Army, the more so as we had 20.000 in one place. 7.000 were in Posavina. They had nothing to do with all that. And then there were some -- a few thousand soldiers in Zepce, Tuzla, and elsewhere. So we didn't even have 40.000 soldiers, but maybe 20.000, 22.000, and we couldn't do anything, because over 50 per cent of our men were holding the lines. So we didn't have a manoeuvring capability. And that was the basis of the assessment of the BH Army, and they had an easy job in Central Bosnia, except for Vitez and Busovaca, where they made a mistake, so they didn't -- because they didn't leave a corridor. If they had left a small corridor, I don't think anybody would have been able to stay there easily as soon as the first civilian had left, but they made a complete circle, they encircled our forces, and in that circle resistance was offered until the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction. On page 85, line 23, the transcript shows that the general was speaking about three small enclaves in the Konjic area, but he was speaking about one enclave with three small villages. The names of these villages were recorded correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Another correction to the transcript. It's really an offensive mistake. On page 87, line 17, Silajdzic -- "not even Silajdzic was able to buy us with 5.000 marks," that's offensive, because that's really a ridiculous sum. I think you spoke about 500.000 marks. Is that not what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is correct. The document reads that we were offered 500.000 marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel. I didn't care about the figure, because nothing was bought eventually.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned Fojnica. When did the ABiH take Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ABiH took complete control over Fojnica until mid-July 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Ms. Alaburic, we had started off in Sovici-Doljani, and I feel that you are getting further and further away from it. Do you plan to come back to that area? If not, I would have another question. But if you plan to come back, I can wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my intentions differ greatly from the reality in this courtroom. I only wanted to show you, by tackling this topic, what kind of combat activity there was and how the territory controlled by the ABiH spread. Triggered by your questions, and it is you who matters -- who mattered the most here, we dealt with the topic of Sovici and Doljani and the responsibility for that, in a very intensive manner. But if you look at my list of topics at the beginning of my first binder, my next topic is Sovici and Doljani, so you will have the opportunity to ask any questions then. Now, I would like to finish dealing with the territories controlled by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: For the record, I was in no way criticising you. Sometimes I have been, but this time, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We are attentive to your criticism; you can be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, when did the ABiH take Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitively on the 2nd of August, 1993. That's when the last HVO soldier left Bugojno, and the civilians who were sent off either -- over Serb-controlled territory or via Vakuf and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When did the ABiH take Vares?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look, in this set of documents, 4D567. 4D567, this is the north of Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. It's the situation in November 1993. We can see the towns conquered by the ABiH, and the numbers next to these towns shows the number of Croats expelled from these areas. Tell us, General, do you know this map?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I know it, only I have a correction. This isn't about towns, but about entire municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's take a look at the area around Mostar. The first document is 4D1216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I don't think this map has been admitted, unless I'm mistaken. Those figures, 25.000, 15.000, 3.000, 12.000, is it just an estimate, or are you absolutely sure of those figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are the figures that were received through the reports of the commanders in these areas and the rough share of the indigenous population and the population that had moved to those areas earlier from areas controlled by the VRS. 1.000 to 2.000 Croats had come to Travnik from VRS-controlled areas, and it was similar with other territories. So there were some indigenous population there and some recent arrivals. They were expelled -- who were expelled from their homes to somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, let us now take a look at the situation in Mostar. Document 4D1216. Tell us, General -- we're about to see the map any moment. In the period up until the 30th of June, 1993, did this communication northward to Jablanica, irrespective of the colour we choose to mark it, was a communication that members of both armies could use?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully, because that was the disposition of forces, the 2nd Brigade, and then the ABiH, and so on all the way to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General -- I believe you remember that General Praljak said in this courtroom that on the 30th of June, 1993, total war broke out in this area between the Muslim and the Croat army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and when I say "Croat army," let me make clear that I mean the BH Croats. Do you agree with this view of General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, total war broke out, and bearing in mind everything that happened before and everything that ensued immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at document 4D622.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this map, General Petkovic, on this map, which you coloured yourself - at least that's what I understood - 4D1216, this the situation before June 30th. I look at Mostar. I see where the HVO is positioned and where the VRS is positioned. Is there a corridor? I already asked this question, anyway, so I don't think it will come to you as a surprise. But is there a small corridor that would make it possible for a person living in East Mostar to squeeze in between the HVO line and the VRS and move upward toward the north, towards the position held by the BH Army? Before June 30th, was that possible, when we look at this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
