utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, it wasn't possible for anyone to pass through the lines. I believe that you mean the situation I'm going to show now [indicates] - could I be assisted - between the positions ... I can't handle this. If anyone can assist me. If you mean this [marks], between the positions, nobody could move there, because these are two lines of fire with soldiers shooting at each other, and whoever would be between there would be shot at. And this area [marks] was only 400 to 500 metres wide, up there a bit wider up to 1.2 kilometres. It was possible to move along arrow number 2, but not between arrow number 1, between the two separated forces which could open fire at each other at any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are saying that it was impossible to go through this line which is marked with a 1; but on the line marked with a 2, it was possible. I have a question dealing with a person living in East Mostar, who would decide to leave East Mostar, was it possible for this person to actually leave East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this moment, yes, because up until the 30th of June free movement was possible northward and southward through the positions of the 2nd HVO Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You say that a Muslim from East Mostar could move through the positions of the 2nd HVO Brigade, could move up north towards the green areas held by the BH Army. So here comes my question: Automatically, would this 2nd HVO Brigade let the Muslims pass through, Muslims who were leaving East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was no reason for this 2nd Brigade to prevent them from doing so because the 2nd Brigade at that moment was manned by both Muslims and Croats. And let me show. This area [marks] was held by the 4th Battalion of the 1st Mostar Brigade, the brigade from Mostar, and there was normal communication between the two areas, although the area was held by the HVO. And if you listen to Mr. Peric, my witness, he said that at this spot, which I'll mark "3" [marks], a telephone connection was set up between the 4th Battalion and the 2nd HVO Brigade, so this was all integrated as a single system of defence of the HVO and the ABiH, and movement was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me sum things up, because it's important for me. You're saying, and you're under oath, that before June 30th a person living in East Mostar could leave East Mostar going through this area controlled by the 2nd HVO Brigade, and you also said that the 2nd Brigade of the HVO at the time was made up of Muslims also, so this person could move up north and could reach the area which you encircled and which represents the 4th Battalion of the BH Army. Let me finish. As far as you know, were there HVO orders that would ban the inhabitants from East Mostar to pass through; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, there weren't any such orders, by no means. I'll add that every command, at their own level, was in a position to decide about how many civilians could move about and in which directions. In times of war, civilians can move from one municipality to another only with the approval of the civilian authorities, because there was a mobilisation order in place under which you were not able to move freely from one municipality to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given the ethnic make-up of the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, is that why you coloured this area both in green and blue? It struck me that there's not just one colour, but there's blue mingled with the green. Is that the reason why you did that, because it was a dual composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the map couldn't be marked blue properly, so some areas appear in pure blue and others stained. I'm sorry, it's for technical reasons I couldn't mark it in pure blue. But we used blue to mark HVO units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if this map was 100 per cent exact, the zone with the 2nd Brigade of the HVO should be only in blue. We see some green, but obviously there were some stains. Very well, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Petkovic, who was the commander of the 2nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilija Vrljic was the commander of the 2nd Brigade, and after him Mr. Stomp ar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber of which ethnicity these commanders were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both were Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I understand this map and what you have commented, it seems to show that Muslims from Mostar, from the east, or even the other river, could move north to the extent that it pleased the Command of the 2nd Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, the commander of the 2nd Brigade didn't decide whether or not they could go or not. That was up to the Wartime Presidency, as it was called, in Eastern Mostar or the Command of the 4th Corps, or the Mostar Brigade of the ABiH, it goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It does not quite go without saying. How can the ABiH Command take any decision which would be binding upon an area which is under the HVO control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, along this line up here [indicates], the brigade kept this communication clear for movement of civilians and all sorts of transportation. There was a reason for the brigade to prevent traffic. Where I marked "1," this is the area of the responsibility of the brigade. The commander will check how many people were sent to pass through this zone, and no more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What is the map you are talking about when you say "number 1"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the map on the screen, where I marked -- to the right, I marked this line with the number 1. I wanted to say that the brigade was responsible for this area, the area in which it held positions against the VRS. The brigade wasn't allowed to seal off a communication line for those who had a right to move along that communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Petkovic, as I interpret the map, there is no road where you have that fresh number 1. That is mountainous area, and it is not a negotiable passage. There's no road, no nothing. It's absolutely theoretical, or am I wrong here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, what I tried to tell you is this: Along the road that exists along the Neretva river, the M-17, the 2nd Brigade at that time shown here was not -- did not take up positions, and I'm telling you where the brigade did have its positions in the hills above. Behind it was the free area of communications where people could move around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I cannot see that from the map. To me, this -- on this map, I see roughly your line number 2 is where the roads are, and they are in an area which is painted blue, which means, as you have explained, that it is -- until point 3, it is under HVO control, so the HVO can decide who passes and who does not, unless I have misunderstood this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point it wasn't the HVO who decided who was going to pass and who wasn't. The 4th Corps and the 1st Brigade could say 200 people are going to travel to Jablanica, for instance, and they will be equipped properly, and set out for Jablanica, and at a check-point we'll see that 400 people are travelling to Jablanica for whatever reason, and there are simply going to pass through -- along that communication road. The brigade has no reason at this point in time to stop anybody, nor was it its task to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Should I just take your word for it, because I do not see it from any document. You are just saying that from your memory, or it's your opinion, or do you have something to support this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, I don't know how far you remember all the documents that we dealt with. Until the 30th of June, the communication towards Jablanica and Konjic was open to everyone, and those who wanted to move along that communication line could do so, both the BH Army members, in their 4th Battalion, and members from the army from Jablanica in the 4th Battalion and Mostar. And at that moment, there were no restrictions, bans, or anything for the 2nd Brigade to say, No, you can't pass. And, similarly, just like the 1st Mostar Brigade, and you see that up here by Mostar, they didn't say the HVO barracks has to leave from this area. No, the HVO barracks remained in the green area. And the soldiers entered the HVO barracks and exited the barracks without the BH Army preventing them from doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to carry on tomorrow, because it's nearly 10 past 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... linked to this map, because I feel it is important, while we're discussing this, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will carry on tomorrow, because it's 10 past 7.00, and we'll have plenty of time tomorrow. So you will be able to take the floor again tomorrow, and I will also ask some questions. So tomorrow we have an afternoon session, so we'll start at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
